AWS DataSync scheduled tasks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Volume Gateway in cached mode stores primary data in S3 and caches frequently accessed data locally as iSCSI block volumes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• File Gateway: file shares (NFS/SMB), not block volumes.
• Tape Gateway: backup tapes.
• DataSync: transfers, not local caching.

Key takeaway: cached block storage → Volume Gateway cached.

stem: A cluster-aware application requires multiple EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone to concurrently read and write to the same block storage volume. Which EBS feature enables this, and what is a key constraint the architect must plan for?

choices.text: EBS snapshots; the volume can be attached to another instance after each snapshot
Elastic Volumes, which automatically prevents write conflicts between instances
EFS mount targets, with each instance placed in a different AZ
EBS Multi-Attach (io1/io2) with a cluster-aware file system

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS Multi-Attach (io1 or io2) lets several instances in one AZ attach the same volume, and a cluster-aware file system coordinates writes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snapshots: not concurrent access.
• Elastic Volumes: resizing.
• EFS across AZs: a file system, not a shared block volume.

Key takeaway: shared block volume in one AZ → Multi-Attach.

stem: An application uploads large video files (5 to 20 GB each) from users distributed globally directly to an S3 bucket in us-east-1. Users in Asia and Australia report slow, inconsistent upload speeds. Which combination of S3 features should the architect implement to improve upload performance without changing the bucket's Region?

choices.text: Switch to the S3 One Zone-IA storage class
Enable S3 Versioning and Cross-Region Replication
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and use multipart upload
Increase the size of the EC2 instance hosting the upload application

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance uploads via edge locations, and multipart upload parallelizes and retries parts of large files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One Zone-IA: storage class.
• Versioning and CRR: after upload.
• Bigger EC2: users upload directly.

Key takeaway: large global uploads → acceleration + multipart.

stem: A big data analytics workload running on hundreds of EC2 instances needs to read and write to a shared EFS file system with the highest possible aggregate throughput and operations per second, and can tolerate slightly higher per-operation latency. Which EFS performance mode should be selected?

choices.text: General Purpose
Provisioned Throughput combined with General Purpose mode
Bursting Throughput
Max I/O

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Max I/O performance mode supports higher aggregate throughput and operations for highly parallel workloads, at slightly higher latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• General Purpose: lower latency, lower scale ceiling.
• Provisioned plus General Purpose: throughput, not operations scale.
• Bursting: throughput mode, not a performance mode.

Key takeaway: massively parallel EFS → Max I/O (or Elastic throughput).

stem: A database on a 500 GiB gp2 volume needs more space and IOPS without downtime. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Enable Multi-Attach and attach a second volume for extra IOPS
Elastic Volumes to gp3, then extend the file system
Detach the volume, snapshot it, and restore to a larger volume
Use Data Lifecycle Manager to resize the volume on a schedule

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Volumes change size, type, and IOPS on attached volumes without detaching them. The OS file system then needs to be extended to use the new space.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snapshot and restore: works but causes downtime.
• Multi-Attach: shares a volume between instances; it doesn't grow capacity.
• DLM: automates snapshots, not resizing.

Key takeaway: change volume size or type online → Elastic Volumes, then grow the file system.

stem: An application on an EC2 instance backed by a 500 GB gp3 volume (at the default baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s) is experiencing high I/O wait times during peak load, and CloudWatch shows the VolumeQueueLength metric consistently elevated. The application cannot tolerate downtime for a volume swap. What is the MOST appropriate immediate remediation?

choices.text: Raise the gp3 volume's IOPS and throughput with Elastic Volumes
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the instance's data transfers
Detach the volume and re-attach it to a larger instance type
Snapshot the volume, restore to a new io2 volume, then swap them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 lets you raise IOPS and throughput with Elastic Volumes online, without detaching or migrating.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: S3.
• Re-attach to a larger instance: doesn't raise volume limits.
• Snapshot to io2: unnecessary downtime.

Key takeaway: gp3 bottleneck → raise provisioned performance online.

stem: A media company needs to run a nightly video transcoding job that processes thousands of files, with individual jobs sometimes running for several hours and requiring GPU instances. Which service is the BEST fit for orchestrating and running this workload?

choices.text: Amazon API Gateway
AWS Step Functions alone, without a compute service
AWS Batch
AWS Lambda

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Batch runs large numbers of batch jobs, including long ones, managing compute and queues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• API Gateway: APIs.
• Step Functions alone: needs compute.
• Lambda: 15-minute limit.

Key takeaway: large batch jobs → AWS Batch.

stem: A genomics research application performs in-memory processing of very large datasets that must be held entirely in RAM, with only moderate CPU and network requirements. Which EC2 instance family is the MOST appropriate starting point?

choices.text: R-family (memory optimized)
I-family (storage optimized)
C-family (compute optimized)
T-family (burstable general purpose)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Memory-optimized R instances provide the RAM needed to hold large datasets in memory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• I-family: local storage.
• C-family: compute.
• T-family: burstable CPU.

Key takeaway: in-memory workloads → R family.

stem: An EC2 Auto Scaling group uses a target tracking policy on average CPU utilization, but CloudWatch metrics show the group repeatedly scaling out and then immediately scaling back in every few minutes, causing instability. What is the MOST likely cause and correct fix?

choices.text: The instance warm-up is too short, so new instances skew the metric; lengthen it
The launch template references an invalid AMI, so new instances fail and are removed
The policy should track network utilization instead of CPU for this workload
The group's maximum size is too low, so scaling oscillates at the upper limit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If warm-up is too short, new instances still initializing skew the CPU metric and cause oscillation. A longer warm-up fixes it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Invalid AMI: instances would fail to launch.
• Network metric: not the issue.
• Low max size: doesn't cause oscillation.

Key takeaway: flapping → instance warm-up.

stem: A nightly Spark job processes 300 TB in S3 for 3 hours. The team wants the lowest cost and no idle cluster between runs. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Batch with custom Spark installed on each job container
Amazon Redshift, loading the 300 TB each night before querying
A permanently running EMR cluster
Transient EMR (or EMR Serverless) with Spot task nodes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR runs Spark natively. Creating the cluster per run (or using EMR Serverless) avoids idle costs, and Spot task nodes cut compute cost for interruptible capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent cluster: pays for idle time 21 hours a day.
• Redshift loads: a warehouse, not a Spark engine; loading 300 TB nightly is wasteful.
• Batch with custom Spark: rebuilds what EMR provides.

Key takeaway: big-data frameworks → EMR; batch cadence → transient or serverless.

stem: A fleet of EC2 instances consumes messages from an SQS standard queue to perform image processing that takes an unpredictable amount of time, sometimes exceeding the queue's default visibility timeout. Workers report receiving and reprocessing messages that another worker is still handling. What should a worker do while it continues processing a message it has already received?

choices.text: Extend the timeout with ChangeMessageVisibility
Switch from SQS to an SNS topic for the work
Reduce the visibility timeout to 0 seconds
Add more consumers polling the same queue

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ChangeMessageVisibility extends the timeout while a message is still being processed, preventing redelivery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS: no work queue.
• Timeout 0: immediate redelivery.
• More consumers: more duplicates.

Key takeaway: long processing → extend visibility.

stem: An application requires single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, a flexible schema, and seamless horizontal scaling to handle unpredictable traffic spikes with no server management, but complex multi-table joins and ACID transactions across many tables are not required. Which database service is the BEST fit?

choices.text: Amazon Redshift
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Aurora Provisioned
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB provides single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, a flexible schema, and horizontal scaling without managing servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift: analytics warehouse.
• Aurora provisioned and RDS PostgreSQL: relational with fixed schemas and scaling limits.

Key takeaway: key-value at any scale → DynamoDB.

stem: A database workload requires a sustained 20,000 IOPS with consistent low-latency performance on an Amazon RDS instance. Which storage configuration should the solutions architect select?

choices.text: General Purpose SSD (gp3) at its default baseline of 3,000 IOPS
Magnetic (standard) storage sized for capacity
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2) at 20,000 IOPS
gp2 sized just large enough to reach 20,000 IOPS with burst credits

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1 or io2) delivers a sustained 20,000 IOPS with consistent latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp3 at baseline: only 3,000 IOPS unless raised.
• Magnetic: legacy and slow.
• gp2 relying on bursts: not sustained.

Key takeaway: sustained IOPS → provisioned IOPS storage.

stem: A solutions architect needs to both improve read scalability for a reporting workload and improve availability during an Availability Zone failure for an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. Which TWO actions together address both goals? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Create one or more read replicas to serve reporting queries
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication on the database's backup bucket
Increase the instance's EBS volume size
Enable a Multi-AZ deployment for automatic failover
Convert the database to a single-AZ deployment with a larger instance type

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas scale reporting reads, and Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby with automatic failover for AZ outages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 CRR on backups: not database availability.
• Bigger EBS: neither goal.
• Single-AZ larger instance: reduces availability.

Key takeaway: read scaling → replicas; AZ failover → Multi-AZ.

stem: A company must migrate a 3 TB Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL. Stored procedures must be converted, and downtime must be under 15 minutes. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Glue to convert the schema and Kinesis to stream the data
Schema Conversion (SCT) plus DMS full load with CDC
Oracle Data Pump export and import during a weekend outage
Restore an Oracle RMAN backup directly into Aurora

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A heterogeneous migration needs schema and code conversion (DMS Schema Conversion or SCT) and a data move with ongoing replication (DMS CDC), so cutover takes minutes once replication lag is near zero.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data Pump: produces Oracle-format dumps and requires long downtime.
• Glue and Kinesis: not a migration toolkit for schema and code conversion.
• RMAN into Aurora: Oracle backups can't be restored into PostgreSQL.

Key takeaway: heterogeneous plus low downtime → schema conversion + DMS CDC.

stem: A development team runs a database that experiences highly variable and infrequent traffic, with near-zero usage between business hours, and wants to avoid paying for idle provisioned capacity while still supporting occasional traffic spikes automatically. Which Aurora configuration is the best fit?

choices.text: A single Aurora Global Database primary cluster
Aurora Serverless v2
Aurora Provisioned with a fixed large instance size
Aurora with manual instance resizing scheduled via cron

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with demand and down during idle periods, matching variable, infrequent traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Global Database: multi-Region replication.
• Fixed large instance: pays when idle.
• Cron resizing: coarse and disruptive.

Key takeaway: variable DB demand → Aurora Serverless v2.

stem: A gaming application backed by DynamoDB requires microsecond read latency for frequently accessed leaderboard data, faster than what DynamoDB alone typically provides. Which service should be added to the architecture?

choices.text: Amazon RDS Proxy
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
DynamoDB Streams
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, replacing DynamoDB entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DAX caches DynamoDB reads in memory for microsecond latency with a DynamoDB-compatible API.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS Proxy: relational connection pooling.
• Streams: change capture.
• Replacing DynamoDB with Redis: a redesign.

Key takeaway: microsecond DynamoDB reads → DAX.

stem: A relational database on Amazon RDS is experiencing consistently high write latency during peak hours, and monitoring shows the WriteIOPS metric near the provisioned limit while CPU and read metrics remain low. Adding read replicas has not improved the situation. What should the architect do to address this write-intensive bottleneck?

choices.text: Enable read replica auto scaling so writes are spread across replicas
Add more read replicas to take write load off the primary
Enable a Multi-AZ deployment so the standby shares the writes
Raise provisioned IOPS, or shard/use NoSQL for write scaling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High write IOPS pressure on the primary needs more provisioned IOPS, or scaling writes horizontally (sharding or a NoSQL store).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replica auto scaling for writes: replicas don't take writes.
• More replicas: same.
• Multi-AZ standby: doesn't share writes.

Key takeaway: write scaling isn't solved by replicas.

stem: A company operates a global gaming platform that uses a custom UDP-based protocol for real-time gameplay, and wants to improve performance and availability for players worldwide by routing traffic over the AWS global network to the optimal endpoint. Which service is the BEST fit?

choices.text: Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing alone
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon CloudFront
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator routes UDP traffic over the AWS network via anycast static IPs to the nearest healthy endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 alone: no network acceleration.
• CloudFront: HTTP(S).
• Transfer Acceleration: S3 uploads.

Key takeaway: UDP acceleration → Global Accelerator.

stem: A single ALB serves api.example.com and www.example.com. On api, /v2/* must go to a new target group; everything else goes to the old one. Which listener rule configuration fits?

choices.text: Cross-zone load balancing with two target groups
Sticky sessions on the new target group
Two separate ALBs with a Route 53 weighted record
Host and path conditions in ordered rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB rules can combine host header and path conditions, evaluated in priority order, so api.example.com + /v2/* reaches the new group and other traffic falls through to later rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two ALBs: unnecessary cost, and DNS weighting can't route by path.
• Sticky sessions: bind users to targets; no routing logic.
• Cross-zone: balances across AZs; no content routing.

Key takeaway: host and path conditions with rule priorities.

stem: A SaaS provider wants to expose an application running behind a Network Load Balancer to hundreds of customer VPCs without requiring VPC peering, without exposing the service over the public internet, and without customers needing to manage IP address overlap concerns. Which AWS feature should the provider use?

choices.text: VPC peering with each customer VPC
AWS PrivateLink (VPC endpoint service)
A public-facing Application Load Balancer with security group restrictions
AWS Site-to-Site VPN to each customer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A PrivateLink endpoint service in front of the NLB lets customers connect through interface endpoints without peering or overlapping-CIDR concerns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering per customer: doesn't scale and exposes networks.
• Public ALB: internet exposure.
• VPN per customer: heavy.

Key takeaway: SaaS to many VPCs → PrivateLink.

stem: The database in a three-tier VPC must download OS patches from the internet but must never accept inbound internet connections. It must also be reachable only from the app tier. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: Private subnet with a route to the internet gateway for patches
Private subnet with no outbound path and patches copied in manually
Public subnet with an Elastic IP and a security group that blocks all inbound
Private subnet via a NAT gateway, with an SG allowing only the app tier's SG

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway provides outbound-only internet access for private subnets, and a security group that references the app tier's group allows only that tier to connect.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public subnet with an EIP: directly addressable from the internet; one misconfiguration exposes it.
• IGW route from a private subnet: makes it public.
• No outbound path: blocks the stated patching requirement.

Key takeaway: outbound only → NAT; inbound only from one tier → SG referencing that tier's SG.

stem: Users report intermittent slow response times from a web application behind an Application Load Balancer spanning three Availability Zones. CloudWatch shows one AZ has significantly more registered targets than the other two, and that AZ's targets show higher average latency and CPU utilization. What is the MOST likely cause and correct fix?

choices.text: Uneven AZ distribution; enable cross-zone load balancing and balance the group
The application needs a Network Load Balancer instead of an Application Load Balancer
The ALB's idle timeout is too high and should be reduced to free connections
The health check interval is too long and should be increased further

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If one AZ has far fewer targets and cross-zone load balancing is off, its targets are overloaded. Enabling cross-zone and balancing the group across AZs evens the load.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB swap: no fix.
• Lower idle timeout: unrelated.
• Longer health check interval: slows detection.

Key takeaway: uneven AZ capacity + no cross-zone = hot targets.

stem: A company runs an application in two AWS Regions behind Application Load Balancers in each Region, and wants to give users a single set of static IP addresses that automatically route to the closest healthy Regional endpoint, with automatic failover to the other Region if one becomes unhealthy, without depending on DNS TTL expiration for failover. Which service should be used?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront with origin failover
AWS Direct Connect Gateway
Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy
AWS Global Accelerator

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs as a single entry point, routing to the nearest healthy Regional ALB with fast failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront origin failover: HTTP caching focus, not static IPs.
• DX gateway: private connectivity.
• Route 53 failover: DNS-based and no static IPs.

Key takeaway: static global entry point → Global Accelerator.

stem: A multiplayer game uses UDP and a custom TCP protocol, needs to see client source IPs, and must support millions of connections with static IPs per AZ. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Classic Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLB handles TCP and UDP at Layer 4 with very high throughput, preserves client source IPs, and supports a static IP or Elastic IP per AZ.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB: HTTP/HTTPS only.
• GWLB: for inserting network appliances, not client traffic distribution.
• CLB: legacy, with no UDP support.

Key takeaway: non-HTTP, source IP preservation, static IPs → NLB.

stem: A global enterprise has a single Direct Connect connection at its headquarters data center and needs to access VPCs located in multiple AWS Regions from that same on-premises connection, without establishing a separate Direct Connect connection in every Region. Which solution enables this?

choices.text: A Direct Connect gateway associated with gateways in multiple Regions
VPC peering between all the Regional VPCs and the headquarters VPC
A separate Site-to-Site VPN from headquarters to each Region
Route 53 Resolver forwarding rules for each Region's VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Direct Connect gateway associates with gateways (VGWs or TGWs) in multiple Regions, extending one connection to VPCs across Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: not for on-premises access.
• VPN per Region: doesn't use DX.
• Resolver rules: DNS only.

Key takeaway: one DX, many Regions → DX gateway.

stem: A company needs to ingest clickstream data in real time, apply custom processing logic to each record within milliseconds of arrival, and allow multiple independent consumer applications to read the same stream of data. Which service should be used for ingestion?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon SQS standard queue
AWS Database Migration Service
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams ingests clickstream in real time and lets custom consumers process each record within milliseconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS: queueing without ordered streaming reads by many consumers.
• DMS: database migration.
• Firehose: buffered delivery, not millisecond custom processing.

Key takeaway: real-time custom stream processing → Kinesis Data Streams.

stem: A data engineering team stores raw clickstream logs in S3 as CSV files and finds that Amazon Athena queries against this data are slow and expensive due to full-file scans. Which change would MOST improve query performance and reduce cost?

choices.text: Increase the S3 bucket's provisioned request throughput
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Move the data to S3 Glacier for faster retrieval
Convert to partitioned Parquet with AWS Glue

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Converting CSV to partitioned Parquet (for example, with Glue) cuts data scanned by Athena, speeding queries and lowering cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Request throughput: not the bottleneck.
• Transfer Acceleration: uploads.
• Glacier: slower.

Key takeaway: Athena performance → columnar + partitions.

stem: 200 TB on an on-premises NFS server must be copied to S3 over a 10 Gbps link, followed by nightly incremental syncs with integrity checks, preserving metadata. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Direct Connect alone, mounting S3 as NFS
S3 Transfer Acceleration with aws s3 sync
AWS Snowball Edge devices every night
AWS DataSync with an on-premises agent

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataSync transfers from NFS or SMB to S3 efficiently, verifies integrity, handles incremental runs on a schedule, and preserves metadata. At 10 Gbps, 200 TB is feasible online in a few days.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Snowball nightly: physical devices suit one-time bulk moves, not daily increments.
• Transfer Acceleration with sync: no built-in scheduling or integrity reporting, and acceleration targets long-distance paths.
• Direct Connect alone: a network link, not a transfer tool, and S3 isn't an NFS server.

Key takeaway: online, repeatable, verified file transfer → DataSync.

stem: Analysts need ad hoc SQL over 50 TB of Parquet in S3, with no servers to manage, and shared interactive dashboards with row-level security by region. Which combination fits BEST?

choices.text: A permanently running EMR cluster with Hive and Grafana
Glue crawlers alone for both querying and dashboards
Load all data into RDS for PostgreSQL and use SNS for dashboards
Athena for SQL, QuickSight with row-level security

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena queries S3 data serverlessly with pay-per-scan pricing, which is ideal for Parquet. QuickSight builds shared dashboards and supports row-level security.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EMR and Grafana: servers to run and no native row-level security for business users.
• RDS and SNS: loading 50 TB into RDS is impractical, and SNS isn't a dashboard tool.
• Glue crawlers: build the catalog but don't run queries or dashboards.

Key takeaway: serverless SQL on S3 → Athena; BI dashboards → QuickSight.

stem: Five teams need access to shared S3 data lake tables: some columns (for example, salary) must be hidden from most teams, and some rows filtered by country. Permissions must be managed centrally. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: IAM policies listing allowed column names
AWS Lake Formation with column and row filters
Separate S3 bucket policies per team and prefix
Amazon Macie with sensitive data findings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lake Formation grants table-, column-, and row-level permissions (data filters) centrally, enforced for integrated engines such as Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket policies: object-level only; can't filter columns or rows.
• IAM policies: can't restrict columns in query results.
• Macie: finds sensitive data; doesn't control access.

Key takeaway: fine-grained data lake access → Lake Formation.

stem: A Kinesis Data Stream is provisioned with 5 shards, each supporting up to 1,000 records per second and 1 MB/s ingestion. Incoming traffic has grown and producers are now experiencing ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors during peak periods, averaging 8,000 records per second at 1.5 KB per record. What should the architect do to resolve this?

choices.text: Increase the data retention period of the stream
Reshard to add shards (UpdateShardCount)
Enable server-side encryption on the stream
Switch consumers from the KCL to the GetRecords API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Throughput beyond the shard capacity needs more shards (UpdateShardCount) or on-demand mode.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retention: storage duration.
• Encryption: security.
• GetRecords instead of KCL: doesn't add ingest capacity.

Key takeaway: ingest limits → add shards.

stem: A company operates a shared S3 bucket that receives data ingested by dozens of separate teams, each of which should only be able to read and write to its own designated prefix within the bucket, using simplified, team-specific access policies rather than one large, complex bucket policy. Which S3 feature should be used?

choices.text: S3 Cross-Region Replication rules per team
S3 Access Points scoped to each team's prefix
S3 Object Lock applied per team prefix
S3 Requester Pays for each team

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 Access Points give each team its own endpoint and policy scoped to its prefix, simplifying permissions on a shared bucket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CRR per team: replication.
• Object Lock per prefix: retention.
• Requester Pays: billing.

Key takeaway: many teams, one bucket → Access Points.

stem: A big data team runs Amazon EMR clusters for Spark ETL jobs and wants to reduce compute costs for the transient, fault-tolerant task nodes that provide additional processing capacity, while ensuring the cluster's core nodes, which hold HDFS data, remain stable. Which approach BEST balances cost and reliability?

choices.text: On-Demand master/core nodes; Spot for task nodes
Spot Instances for all node types, including core nodes
The smallest On-Demand instance type for the whole cluster
Reserved Instances for every node in the cluster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Keep master and core nodes (which hold HDFS data) On-Demand, and use Spot for task nodes that only compute, cutting cost without risking data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Spot for core nodes: data loss risk.
• Smallest instances: slow jobs.
• RIs for transient clusters: pay when idle.

Key takeaway: EMR: Spot for task nodes.

stem: An AWS Glue ETL job that processes daily ingested data from S3 has become increasingly slow over several months. Investigation reveals that the source S3 prefix now contains millions of very small files, a few KB each, instead of fewer, larger files, causing excessive job planning time and per-file processing overhead. What is the MOST effective fix for this small file problem?

choices.text: Add a compaction step that merges small files before the ETL job
Rewrite the job from PySpark to Scala to reduce per-file overhead
Disable job bookmarks so files are read in larger batches
Keep increasing the job's DPUs as the number of files grows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Many small files slow Spark jobs because of per-file overhead. Compacting them into fewer, larger files restores performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scala rewrite: doesn't remove per-file overhead.
• Disabling bookmarks: reprocesses data.
• More DPUs: costly and treats the symptom.

Key takeaway: small-files problem → compaction.

stem: A public research dataset in S3 is downloaded heavily by outside institutions with AWS accounts. The owner wants downloaders to pay for request and transfer costs, and wants to block anonymous access. Which setting fits?

choices.text: Enable Cross-Region Replication to the users' Regions
Serve the data through CloudFront with signed URLs
Enable Requester Pays
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With Requester Pays, the requester pays for requests and data transfer. Requests must be authenticated, so anonymous downloads aren't allowed, which matches the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speeds transfers and adds cost to the owner.
• Replication: adds storage cost for the owner.
• CloudFront signed URLs: control access, but the owner still pays delivery costs.

Key takeaway: shift download costs to requesters → Requester Pays.

stem: A company manages AWS accounts for multiple business units under AWS Organizations and wants to allocate shared services costs to each business unit's cost center for chargeback reporting. Which combination of actions should a solutions architect recommend? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Analyze the Cost and Usage Report by tag
Enable S3 Requester Pays on shared buckets so teams pay directly
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks for each business unit
Create one consolidated CloudWatch dashboard of estimated charges
Apply and activate cost allocation tags

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Activated cost allocation tags label shared costs, and the Cost and Usage Report grouped by tag supports allocation to business units.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requester Pays: shifts some S3 costs only.
• Trusted Advisor: recommendations.
• Estimated-charges dashboard: no allocation.

Key takeaway: cost allocation → tags + CUR.

stem: A team wants an email when forecast monthly spend will exceed $10,000, and also wants a Slack alert when actual spend passes 80% of that budget. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Cost and Usage Report delivered to S3
AWS Budgets forecast and actual alerts
AWS Cost Explorer saved reports
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Budgets supports thresholds on forecast and actual spend and notifies through email or SNS, which can feed Slack via AWS Chatbot.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer: analysis, not proactive alerts.
• CUR: detailed billing data files; no alerting.
• Trusted Advisor: optimization tips; no budget alerts.

Key takeaway: thresholds and alerts on spend → Budgets.

stem: A company uses AWS Backup to protect RDS and EBS resources and wants to minimize long-term backup storage costs while retaining backups for 7 years for compliance. What should the solutions architect configure?

choices.text: AWS Backup lifecycle rules to cold storage
Scripts that copy backups to S3 Glacier on a schedule
Disable backups after 90 days to reduce cost
Keep all backups in warm storage indefinitely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Backup lifecycle rules transition backups to cold storage after a period, lowering long-term cost while keeping retention.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom scripts to Glacier: unsupported and fragile.
• Disabling backups: violates retention.
• Warm storage forever: expensive.

Key takeaway: long retention cost → Backup lifecycle to cold storage.

stem: A database needs a steady 6,000 IOPS and 250 MB/s on a 400 GiB volume at the lowest cost. Which EBS configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: gp2 at 2 TiB to earn the IOPS from size
st1 throughput-optimized HDD
io2 with 6,000 provisioned IOPS
gp3 with provisioned IOPS and throughput

explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of size at a lower price than io2, and 6,000 IOPS and 250 MB/s are within its limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• gp2 at 2 TiB: pays for unneeded capacity to get IOPS.
• io2: meets it but costs more; its extra durability and latency consistency aren't required here.
• st1: HDD for sequential throughput with low IOPS.

Key takeaway: moderate provisioned performance → gp3.

stem: A company needs to continuously and automatically synchronize large volumes of files from an on-premises NFS file server to Amazon S3 on a recurring schedule, with minimal ongoing operational management. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this task?

choices.text: AWS Storage Gateway (Tape Gateway)
AWS Snowball
AWS Transfer Family
AWS DataSync

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataSync continuously and efficiently synchronizes NFS data to AWS storage on a schedule, with integrity checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tape Gateway: backups.
• Snowball: offline one-time moves.
• Transfer Family: SFTP.

Key takeaway: ongoing NFS sync → DataSync.

stem: A company notices a large, unexpected increase in Amazon S3 data transfer charges after enabling Cross-Region Replication (CRR) from its primary bucket in us-east-1 to a disaster recovery bucket in eu-west-1. What is the most cost-effective way to reduce these charges while still meeting the disaster recovery requirement?

choices.text: Switch from Cross-Region Replication to Same-Region Replication
Replicate only the prefixes or tags needed for DR
Disable versioning on the source bucket
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Filtering replication rules to only the prefixes or tags needed for DR reduces the volume replicated and the transfer charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same-Region Replication: loses Regional DR.
• Disabling versioning: breaks replication.
• Transfer Acceleration: adds cost.

Key takeaway: replicate only what DR needs.

stem: A bucket holds 800 million objects averaging 2 MB with unknown, shifting access patterns. Some become hot again after months. The team wants automatic savings with no retrieval fees for the automatic tiers. Which class fits?

choices.text: S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 One Zone-IA

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers based on usage and moves them back when accessed, with no retrieval fees for its automatic tiers. A small monitoring fee per object applies, which is acceptable at 2 MB average size.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard-IA: retrieval fees add up when objects become hot again.
• Glacier Flexible Retrieval: slow retrieval.
• One Zone-IA: less resilient, and it has retrieval fees.

Key takeaway: unknown or changing access → Intelligent-Tiering.

stem: A video transcoding queue can pause and resume jobs from checkpoints, with no deadline tighter than 24 hours. Which EC2 purchasing strategy minimizes cost while limiting interruptions?

choices.text: Standard Reserved Instances for peak capacity
On-Demand Instances of one instance type
Diversified Spot, price-capacity-optimized
Dedicated Hosts purchased for three years

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spot provides the largest discount for interruptible work, and diversifying instance types and AZs with price-capacity-optimized allocation draws from deep pools to reduce interruptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-Demand: pays full price for flexible work.
• Dedicated Hosts: expensive and meant for licensing or compliance needs.
• Reserved for peak: commits to capacity idle most of the time.

Key takeaway: interruptible and flexible → diversified Spot.

stem: A company has a steady-state fleet of EC2 instances running a mix of instance families and sizes across multiple AWS accounts, and workloads may shift between instance types over the next three years. Which purchasing option provides savings while maximizing flexibility across instance family and size changes?

choices.text: Zonal Reserved Instances
Compute Savings Plans
Standard Reserved Instances
EC2 Instance Savings Plans

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, sizes, Regions, and accounts in the organization, fitting a mixed fleet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Zonal RIs: tied to AZ and type.
• Standard RIs: tied to family and Region.
• EC2 Instance Savings Plans: tied to family and Region.

Key takeaway: mixed fleets → Compute Savings Plans.

stem: A solutions architect wants to identify EC2 instances that are consistently underutilized so the company can downsize them to a smaller instance size and reduce costs. Which AWS service provides automated instance right-sizing recommendations based on utilization metrics?

choices.text: AWS Config
AWS Compute Optimizer
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization and recommends smaller instance types for underused instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration.
• Trusted Advisor: some low-utilization checks, less specific.
• Logs Insights: logs.

Key takeaway: rightsizing → Compute Optimizer.

stem: A company runs 25 HTTP microservices. It wants one entry point with path routing, TLS termination with ACM, and authentication against an OIDC provider at the load balancer, at low cost. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: One ALB with path rules and OIDC auth
A Network Load Balancer per microservice
A Classic Load Balancer per microservice
A Gateway Load Balancer with 25 target groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single ALB can hold many listener rules for path routing, terminate TLS with ACM, and authenticate users through OIDC or Cognito, so one load balancer covers all services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB per service: 25 load balancers, and no path routing or OIDC.
• CLB: legacy, with no path routing or OIDC.
• GWLB: for network appliances, not HTTP routing.

Key takeaway: many HTTP services behind one entry point → one ALB with rules.

stem: A company's e-commerce application experiences predictable traffic patterns, with high demand during business hours on weekdays and very low demand overnight and on weekends. How can the company reduce EC2 costs while maintaining the ability to handle peak load?

choices.text: Move the workload to a single large EC2 instance running continuously
Purchase Reserved Instances sized for the peak capacity
Keep enough On-Demand instances running at all times for peak load
Auto Scaling with scheduled actions for low-demand periods

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Auto Scaling with scheduled actions reduces capacity during predictable low-demand periods and raises it for business hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single large instance: no elasticity.
• RIs for peak: pay for idle.
• Peak On-Demand always: overpay.

Key takeaway: predictable patterns → scheduled scaling.

stem: A development team spins up EC2 instances each morning to run stateful test environments and shuts them down each evening, but restarting applications and reloading in-memory state takes considerable time. Which EC2 feature reduces this startup time while still saving on costs when the instance is not in use?

choices.text: EC2 Dedicated Instances
EC2 hibernation
EC2 Auto Scaling termination policies
EC2 Spot Fleet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hibernation saves memory to the EBS root volume on stop, so stateful test environments resume where they left off.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated Instances: tenancy.
• Termination policies: scaling behavior.
• Spot Fleet: pricing.

Key takeaway: resume state after stop → hibernation.

stem: A manufacturing company needs to run low-latency compute workloads on-premises at a factory location that has strict data residency and latency requirements, while still using the same APIs, tools, and billing model as AWS in the cloud. Which AWS service should the solutions architect recommend?

choices.text: AWS Outposts
AWS Local Zones
AWS Wavelength
AWS Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outposts runs AWS infrastructure on premises at the factory, meeting data residency and low-latency needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Local Zones: AWS-operated metro locations, not the factory.
• Wavelength: 5G carrier edge.
• Direct Connect: connectivity only.

Key takeaway: AWS compute on-premises → Outposts.

stem: A company runs containerized batch-processing jobs on Amazon ECS that can tolerate interruptions. Which capacity provider strategy would most reduce compute costs?

choices.text: EC2 On-Demand instances run outside of Auto Scaling
A capacity provider strategy favoring Fargate Spot
Only Reserved Instances for the cluster's EC2 capacity
Fargate with On-Demand pricing for every task

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A capacity provider strategy favoring Fargate Spot runs interruptible tasks at a large discount.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-Demand without scaling: costly.
• RIs only: commitment for batch.
• Fargate On-Demand for all: no discount.

Key takeaway: interruptible containers → Fargate Spot.

stem: A global company wants to reduce the compute cost and latency of processing user image uploads for a website distributed through Amazon CloudFront by performing lightweight resizing logic closer to end users, instead of running dedicated servers in a central region. Which AWS service enables this?

choices.text: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
AWS Batch
Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Functions
AWS Outposts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Functions run code at edge locations close to users, reducing latency for lightweight request processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 Auto Scaling, Batch, Outposts: not at CloudFront edges.

Key takeaway: edge processing → Lambda@Edge / CloudFront Functions.

stem: A company wants to choose a load balancer for deploying third-party network security and firewall virtual appliances transparently in front of its VPC traffic, in the most cost-efficient way to inspect traffic at scale. Which load balancer type is designed for this purpose?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway Load Balancer transparently deploys and scales third-party network appliances in the traffic path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB, CLB, NLB: not transparent appliance insertion.

Key takeaway: inline appliances → GWLB.

stem: A startup's DynamoDB table serves a new application with highly unpredictable and spiky traffic that is difficult to forecast, and the team wants to avoid throttling while minimizing cost during idle periods. Which DynamoDB capacity mode should be used?

choices.text: On-Demand capacity mode
Provisioned capacity with Auto Scaling set to a high fixed minimum
DynamoDB Reserved Capacity
Provisioned capacity with no Auto Scaling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
On-demand capacity mode handles unpredictable spikes without capacity planning, charging per request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• High fixed minimum: overpays.
• Reserved capacity: for steady usage.
• No auto scaling: throttles on spikes.

Key takeaway: unpredictable DynamoDB traffic → on-demand.

stem: A company is designing a new application that will store simple key-value user session data with extremely high request rates, hundreds of thousands of requests per second, and needs to minimize operational and infrastructure cost at that scale. Which database approach is most cost-effective?

choices.text: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Redshift
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with a large Multi-AZ instance
Amazon RDS for MySQL with read replicas

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB handles simple key-value session data at very high request rates with low latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift: analytics.
• Large RDS instances: relational overhead and scaling limits.

Key takeaway: high-rate key-value → DynamoDB.

stem: A regulated app must keep 10 years of transactions queryable on demand, but rows older than 2 years are rarely read. The RDS database is growing expensively. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Delete rows older than 2 years
Increase the RDS storage size for all 10 years
Archive old rows to S3 and query with Athena
Move the database to a larger instance class

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exporting old data to S3 in a columnar format keeps it cheap and durable while still queryable on demand with Athena, and the primary database shrinks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger storage: keeps paying database prices for cold data.
• Deleting: violates the 10-year retention requirement.
• Bigger instance: adds compute cost without addressing storage.

Key takeaway: hot data in the database, cold data in S3 with query-in-place.

stem: A company's internal application has highly variable database usage, with near-zero traffic on nights and weekends and moderate traffic during business hours. The company wants a relational database that automatically scales capacity up and down, including scaling to near-zero, so it only pays for capacity used. Which option should the solutions architect recommend?

choices.text: Amazon RDS for MySQL with a fixed-size Multi-AZ instance
Amazon DynamoDB with provisioned capacity
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2
Amazon Redshift with Concurrency Scaling

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Serverless v2 scales database capacity down during idle nights and weekends and up for business hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fixed RDS: pays when idle.
• DynamoDB provisioned: different model and fixed capacity.
• Redshift: analytics.

Key takeaway: variable relational load → Aurora Serverless v2.

stem: A company runs a commercial relational database engine on Amazon RDS and pays high license fees. To reduce total cost of ownership, the company wants to move to an open-source-compatible engine with minimal application code changes, using an AWS-managed migration approach. What should the solutions architect do?

choices.text: Rebuild the entire application from scratch on DynamoDB
Resize the existing RDS instance to a smaller class
Export and import the data manually with custom scripts
Migrate to Aurora with DMS and SCT

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Migrating from a commercial engine to Aurora with DMS (data) and SCT (schema and code) removes license fees.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rebuild on DynamoDB: major rewrite.
• Smaller instance: license fees remain.
• Manual scripts: risky.

Key takeaway: cut license costs → migrate to Aurora with DMS + SCT.

stem: A new RDS database needs 8,000 IOPS steadily and can tolerate occasional latency variation. Cost matters. Which storage option fits BEST?

choices.text: io1 storage, since production databases require Provisioned IOPS
io2 Block Express for the lowest possible latency
Magnetic storage, since it's the cheapest option
gp3 storage with 8,000 provisioned IOPS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 lets you provision IOPS separately from size at lower cost. io1 and io2 are for workloads that need very high IOPS or the most consistent latency, which isn't required here.

Why the other options are wrong:
• io1: pricier and not required for production by any rule.
• Magnetic: legacy, with low performance.
• io2 Block Express: exceeds the need at higher cost.

Key takeaway: pick the cheapest storage that meets the performance requirement.

stem: A company's DynamoDB costs have risen significantly, and monitoring shows that a frequently run application query performs a full table Scan operation to find items matching a non-key attribute. What is the most cost-effective fix?

choices.text: Switch to On-Demand capacity mode and keep the Scan
Enable DAX write-through caching on the table
Increase the table's provisioned write capacity
Add a GSI and use Query instead of Scan

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A full table Scan reads every item. A GSI on the queried attribute lets the application use Query, reading only matching items.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand with Scan: still expensive.
• DAX: caches but still scans on misses.
• More write capacity: unrelated.

Key takeaway: frequent Scans → design an index and Query.

stem: A non-production VPC has NAT gateways in three AZs, and costs are high. Some downtime of outbound access during an AZ failure is acceptable, and cross-AZ data charges should stay low. Which change fits BEST?

choices.text: Add a second NAT gateway in each AZ for redundancy
One NAT gateway plus S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints
Replace the NAT gateways with an egress-only internet gateway
Route the private subnets directly to the internet gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
One NAT gateway cuts the hourly cost by two thirds, accepting reduced resilience in non-production. Gateway endpoints remove S3 and DynamoDB traffic from the NAT path, reducing processing and cross-AZ charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More NAT gateways: increases cost.
• Direct IGW routes: makes subnets public.
• Egress-only gateway: IPv6 only.

Key takeaway: match redundancy to environment criticality, and remove traffic from NAT where endpoints exist.

stem: A company has 25 VPCs across multiple AWS accounts that all need to communicate with each other and with a shared services VPC, and the network topology is expected to keep growing. Using full-mesh VPC peering has become operationally complex and costly to manage. What should the solutions architect implement instead to simplify connectivity while controlling cost as scale grows?

choices.text: Deploy an AWS Transit Gateway and attach each VPC to it
Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection between every VPC pair
Continue adding more individual VPC peering connections between every pair of VPCs
Use AWS Direct Connect to connect all the VPCs together

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Transit Gateway connects all 25 VPCs and the shared services VPC in a hub-and-spoke model, replacing a growing mesh.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPN between pairs: unmanageable.
• More peering: doesn't scale.
• Direct Connect: for on-premises links.

Key takeaway: many VPCs → Transit Gateway.

stem: A company wants example.com (the zone apex) to point to an ALB and cdn.example.com to CloudFront, without paying for those DNS queries. Which record types fit?

choices.text: CNAME records for both names
TXT records containing the target DNS names
Alias A (and AAAA) records for both names
A CNAME for cdn and an A record with the ALB's IP for the apex

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alias records work at the zone apex, track the target's changing IPs, and queries to alias records pointing at AWS resources are free.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CNAMEs: not allowed at the zone apex, and CNAME queries are billed.
• Hardcoded ALB IP: ALB IPs change.
• TXT records: don't route traffic.

Key takeaway: AWS targets and zone apex → alias records.

stem: A media company serves large video files and images from an S3 bucket to a global user base, resulting in high data transfer out costs directly from S3 and slow load times for distant users. What is the most effective way to reduce both data transfer costs and latency?

choices.text: Move the S3 bucket to a Region closer to the average user
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Put Amazon CloudFront in front of the bucket
Enable S3 Requester Pays for downloads

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches content at edge locations, reducing latency and origin data transfer costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move the bucket: one Region can't be close to everyone.
• Transfer Acceleration: uploads and costs more.
• Requester Pays: unsuitable for public users.

Key takeaway: global delivery → CloudFront.

stem: A company deploys an application with EC2 instances spread across three Availability Zones within a single Region, and instances frequently communicate with each other for processing. After reviewing the bill, the company finds unexpectedly high data transfer charges. What is the most likely cause and cost-effective fix?

choices.text: CloudFront is not enabled
The VPC uses an internet gateway, which charges for internal traffic
Cross-AZ traffic; keep chatty components in the same AZ
Traffic between AZs uses the public internet; add a NAT gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-AZ data transfer is charged. Keeping chatty components in the same AZ (while preserving multi-AZ resilience at the tier level) cuts that cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront: unrelated.
• IGW charges internal traffic: it doesn't.
• Traffic uses the internet: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: chatty cross-AZ traffic costs money.

stem: FinOps must build a custom allocation model using per-resource, hourly line items for data transfer and NAT charges over the last 3 months, queried with SQL. Which source fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Budgets reports emailed weekly
CUR in S3, queried with Athena
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
Cost Explorer grouped by service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CUR (or Data Exports) delivers the most detailed billing data, including resource IDs and hourly granularity, to S3, where Athena can query it with SQL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Budgets reports: summaries against thresholds.
• Cost Explorer: aggregated views without full line-item detail for custom models.
• Trusted Advisor: recommendations, not billing data.

Key takeaway: line-item billing analytics → CUR + Athena.

stem: A global company has application servers in multiple AWS Regions that occasionally need to transfer large datasets between Regions for processing, resulting in significant inter-region data transfer costs. Which architectural change would best reduce these costs?

choices.text: Process data in the Region where it is stored
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication for all buckets
Use Direct Connect between each pair of Regions
Increase the size of the EC2 instances in each Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Processing data in the Region where it's stored avoids inter-Region transfer charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replicate everything: more transfer.
• DX between Regions: not how Regions connect.
• Bigger instances: unrelated.

Key takeaway: move compute to data.

stem: An application deployed behind an Application Load Balancer intermittently loses users' shopping cart contents after requests are routed to a different EC2 instance than the one that started the session. What is the MOST scalable fix?

choices.text: Enable sticky sessions on the ALB and increase the instance count
Switch to a Network Load Balancer to keep source IP affinity
Reduce the ALB idle timeout
Keep cart state in DynamoDB or ElastiCache

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Storing cart state in DynamoDB or ElastiCache makes instances stateless, so any instance can serve any request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sticky sessions: carts lost when instances fail.
• NLB: doesn't fix state.
• Lower idle timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: externalize session state.

stem: A microservice repeatedly calls a failing third-party payment API, and each failed call still takes 10 seconds to time out, causing cascading slowdowns and connection pool exhaustion in the calling service. Which pattern should be implemented to prevent this cascading failure?

choices.text: Increase the timeout to 30 seconds so more calls can complete
Increase the number of retry attempts for each failed call
Remove error handling so failures reach the client immediately
A circuit breaker that fails fast after a failure threshold

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A circuit breaker fails fast after repeated failures, preventing threads from waiting on timeouts, and retries later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeout: worse.
• More retries: worse.
• Removing error handling: breaks behavior.

Key takeaway: failing dependency → circuit breaker.

stem: A DynamoDB table storing daily transaction logs uses the transaction date, such as 2026-09-15, as the partition key. During peak hours, the table experiences frequent ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors even though the table's overall provisioned capacity has headroom. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The AWS Region has insufficient DynamoDB capacity for the table
DynamoDB Streams is not enabled, so writes are not distributed
The table's sort key is missing
A day's writes hit one partition key value (hot partition)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Using the date as partition key sends a whole day's writes to one key value, creating a hot partition.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Region capacity: not the cause.
• Streams: unrelated.
• Missing sort key: not the cause.

Key takeaway: low-cardinality partition keys create hot spots.

stem: A developer needs to run AWS CLI commands against two different AWS accounts from the same workstation without repeatedly re-entering credentials. What should they configure?

choices.text: A single IAM user shared between both accounts
Named CLI profiles selected with --profile
A bearer token stored in an environment variable
Two separate installations of the AWS CLI

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Named profiles in the CLI config store separate credentials or role settings, selected with --profile.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared IAM user: poor practice.
• Bearer token: not how the CLI authenticates.
• Two installations: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: multiple accounts in the CLI → named profiles.

stem: An application connects to an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance, and the security team requires that all connections use SSL/TLS. Developers report that some client connections still succeed without SSL. What should be done to fully enforce encrypted connections?

choices.text: Enforce SSL with require_secure_transport in the parameter group
Enable RDS storage encryption on the instance
Rotate the RDS master password regularly
Enable a Multi-AZ deployment for the instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Setting require_secure_transport in the DB parameter group forces all MySQL connections to use SSL/TLS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Storage encryption: at rest.
• Password rotation: authentication.
• Multi-AZ: availability.

Key takeaway: enforce TLS on RDS MySQL → parameter group.

stem: A developer needs to store a frequently changing, hierarchically organized set of non-secret configuration values that several Lambda functions read at runtime, and wants to update those values without redeploying any function code. Compared to Lambda environment variables, why might AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store be the better fit?

choices.text: Lambda environment variables cannot be encrypted under any circumstances
Parameter Store values change without redeploying functions and support hierarchies
Parameter Store is the only mechanism that can pass values into a Lambda function
Lambda environment variables can store only numeric values

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parameter Store supports hierarchical paths, and values can change without redeploying functions that read them at runtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Env vars can't be encrypted: they can.
• Only mechanism: env vars also work.
• Env vars numeric only: false.

Key takeaway: shared, changing, hierarchical config → Parameter Store.

stem: Account A owns an S3 bucket encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key in account A. A role in account B has an identity policy allowing s3:GetObject on the bucket, and the bucket policy grants that role s3:GetObject. Downloads from account B still fail with AccessDenied. Which TWO changes are required? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Add kms:Decrypt on the key ARN to the account B role's identity policy.
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so replicated objects are readable.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for cross-account downloads.
Switch the bucket to SSE-S3 managed from account B.
Allow the account B role in the account A key policy.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account SSE-KMS reads need two permissions: the key policy in Account A must allow Account B's role, and the role's identity policy must allow kms:Decrypt on the key ARN.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning: unrelated.
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• SSE-S3 from B: can't change A's encryption.

Key takeaway: cross-account KMS = key policy + identity policy.

stem: A bucket stores sensitive reports. The company requires that objects can only be accessed from applications in one specific VPC, even by IAM users who have s3:* permissions. What should the solutions architect configure?

choices.text: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the bucket.
A bucket policy that denies access unless aws:SourceVpce matches the endpoint.
A network ACL on the private subnets allowing only the S3 prefix list.
A security group on the bucket that allows only the VPC CIDR.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy denying access unless aws:SourceVpce matches the VPC endpoint ensures objects are reachable only through that endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object Lock: retention.
• NACL with prefix list: doesn't restrict who else can access.
• Security group on a bucket: buckets don't have SGs.

Key takeaway: restrict S3 to one VPC → aws:SourceVpce condition.

stem: A mobile app lets signed-in users upload photos directly to S3. Each user must be able to read and write only objects under their own prefix, and the app must not embed long-term AWS credentials. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.text: Make the bucket public and rely on long, unguessable object keys.
Create one IAM user per app user and distribute their keys at sign-up.
Embed an IAM access key in the app and prefix objects with the user's email.
Cognito identity pool credentials with a per-user prefix policy variable.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cognito identity pool credentials with an IAM policy using the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} variable limit each user to their own prefix.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public bucket: insecure.
• IAM user per app user: unmanageable.
• Embedded key with email prefix: shared secret and weak.

Key takeaway: per-user S3 access for app users → identity pools + policy variables.

stem: A public web application behind an ALB is receiving SQL injection attempts and occasional request floods where single IP addresses send thousands of requests per minute. Which solution addresses both issues with the least operational effort?

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty with automatic blocking enabled for the ALB.
Network ACL deny rules added for each attacking IP address.
Security group rules that deny attacking IPs as they are discovered.
A WAF web ACL with the SQL managed rule group and a rate-based rule.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A WAF web ACL with the SQL database managed rule group blocks SQL injection, and a rate-based rule blocks IPs sending too many requests.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty: detects, doesn't block at the ALB.
• NACL per IP: manual.
• SG deny rules: SGs can't deny.

Key takeaway: SQLi + floods → WAF managed rules + rate-based rules.

stem: An application stores its RDS database password in a configuration file. Security requires the password to be rotated automatically every 30 days without application downtime and without custom rotation code. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Secrets Manager with managed RDS rotation, read at runtime.
Encrypt the configuration file with KMS and redeploy the application each month.
Use an EC2 instance role so that no database password is needed for any engine.
Store the password as a Parameter Store SecureString and update it manually.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager rotates RDS passwords automatically, and the application reads the current secret at runtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• KMS file with redeploys: manual.
• Instance role alone: DB still needs credentials (unless IAM DB auth).
• Parameter Store manual updates: no rotation.

Key takeaway: rotating DB credentials → Secrets Manager.

stem: Workers poll an SQS standard queue. Each message takes up to 90 seconds to process. The queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. The team notices many messages are processed two or three times. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?

choices.text: Messages reappear before processing ends; raise the visibility timeout.
The queue should be FIFO, because standard queues deliver each message three times.
Long polling is disabled; enable a 20-second receive wait time on the queue.
The message retention period is too short; increase it to the 14-day maximum.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With a 30-second visibility timeout and 90-second processing, messages reappear and are processed again. Raise the timeout above processing time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• FIFO: standard delivers at least once, but the issue is the timeout.
• Long polling: unrelated.
• Retention: unrelated.

Key takeaway: visibility timeout > processing time.

stem: A MySQL workload needs automatic failover typically under 35 seconds and also needs to offload read queries to standby instances that are already provisioned for high availability. Which RDS deployment option meets these requirements?

choices.text: Single-AZ instance with a cross-Region read replica for reads.
Single-AZ instance with automated backups and fast restore.
Multi-AZ DB cluster with two readable standbys.
Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with one standby for reads.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standbys and typically fails over in under 35 seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cross-Region replica: not automatic failover.
• Backups: slow restore.
• Multi-AZ DB instance: standby isn't readable.

Key takeaway: fast failover + readable standbys → Multi-AZ DB cluster.

stem: Users of a web application behind an ALB are logged out whenever the Auto Scaling group scales in. Sessions are stored in each instance's memory. The team wants sessions to survive scaling events without pinning users to instances. What should it do?

choices.text: Disable scale-in on the Auto Scaling group during business hours.
Keep session state in ElastiCache or DynamoDB.
Increase the target group deregistration delay to 1 hour.
Enable sticky sessions on the ALB target group.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Moving sessions to ElastiCache or DynamoDB makes instances stateless, so scale-in doesn't log users out.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable scale-in: wastes money.
• Long deregistration delay: sessions still lost at termination.
• Sticky sessions: still lost when instances terminate.

Key takeaway: stateless instances survive scaling.

stem: A Lambda function processes records from a Kinesis data stream. One malformed record causes the function to fail, and the shard stops making progress for hours while Lambda retries the same batch. Which configuration resolves this while keeping failed records for analysis?

choices.text: Bisect on error, cap retries, and add an on-failure destination.
Set the batch size to 10,000 records so the bad record is diluted.
Increase the function timeout and memory so the batch can finish.
Increase the number of shards so other records keep flowing.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bisect-on-error splits the batch to isolate the bad record, a retry cap stops endless retries, and an on-failure destination captures it so the shard moves on.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Larger batch: the bad record still fails the batch.
• More timeout and memory: doesn't fix bad data.
• More shards: the stuck shard remains stuck.

Key takeaway: poison records in streams → bisect, limit retries, send to a destination.

stem: A company wants users to see a static maintenance page hosted in S3 automatically if its primary web application in us-east-1 becomes unhealthy. Which Route 53 configuration achieves this?

choices.text: Simple routing with two IP addresses in one record.
Geolocation routing with a default record pointing to S3.
Failover routing with a health check and an S3 secondary record.
Latency-based routing between the application and the S3 website.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Failover routing with a health check on the primary returns the S3 website record as secondary when the application is unhealthy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing: no health-based failover.
• Geolocation default: not health-based.
• Latency: sends some users to the maintenance page all the time.

Key takeaway: automatic maintenance page → failover record to S3.

stem: A database on EC2 needs 12,000 IOPS on a 200 GiB volume. The team wants the lowest cost EBS option that meets this requirement without over-provisioning storage. Which volume type should it choose?

choices.text: io2 Block Express, 4 TiB, for guaranteed IOPS.
st1 throughput-optimized HDD, 200 GiB.
gp2, 200 GiB, relying on burst credits.
gp3, 200 GiB, with 12,000 provisioned IOPS.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 lets you provision 12,000 IOPS on a 200 GiB volume independently of size, at lower cost than io2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• io2 at 4 TiB: overprovisioned and costly.
• st1: HDD.
• gp2 with bursts: 200 GiB gives only 600 baseline IOPS.

Key takeaway: provisioned IOPS without size → gp3.

stem: A DynamoDB table uses a date string (YYYY-MM-DD) as the partition key for IoT readings. All writes for the current day go to one partition key, causing throttling even though table-level capacity is not exhausted. What is the BEST fix?

choices.text: Use a high-cardinality key or write sharding.
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode.
Add a global secondary index on the date attribute to spread the writes.
Add DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table to absorb the writes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A high-cardinality partition key (for example, device ID) or write sharding with suffixes spreads writes across partitions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand: doesn't fix a hot key.
• GSI on date: has the same hot key.
• DAX: caches reads, not writes.

Key takeaway: hot key → higher cardinality or sharding.

stem: A multiplayer game uses UDP servers in three Regions. Players worldwide need low, consistent latency, and firewall rules at partner networks require a small set of fixed IP addresses. Which service meets these requirements?

choices.text: Route 53 latency-based routing to Elastic IPs in each Region.
AWS Global Accelerator with Regional endpoint groups.
An Application Load Balancer in each Region behind DNS.
Amazon CloudFront with the game servers as custom origins.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs for partner allow lists and routes UDP traffic to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint group.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 to EIPs: IP lists per Region and no network acceleration.
• ALBs: no UDP.
• CloudFront: not for UDP game servers.

Key takeaway: static IPs + UDP + global → Global Accelerator.

stem: A genomics team runs HPC jobs on hundreds of Linux instances that need a shared POSIX file system with hundreds of GB/s throughput. Input data lives in S3, and results must be written back to S3. Which storage fits BEST?

choices.text: EBS Multi-Attach volumes shared by all instances in the cluster.
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with SMB multichannel.
Amazon EFS in Max I/O mode with provisioned throughput.
FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FSx for Lustre provides a POSIX file system with hundreds of GB/s throughput for HPC and integrates with S3 data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS Multi-Attach: few instances, one AZ.
• FSx for Windows: SMB.
• EFS Max I/O: lower peak throughput than Lustre for HPC.

Key takeaway: HPC shared file system → FSx for Lustre.

stem: Analysts query 5 TB of CSV logs in S3 with Athena. Most queries filter by date and read only 4 of 60 columns, yet each query scans the full dataset and is slow and costly. Which change provides the biggest improvement?

choices.text: Convert to Parquet and partition by date.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the log bucket.
Compress the existing CSV files with ZIP.
Move the data to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parquet lets Athena read only 4 of 60 columns, and date partitions prune files, reducing data scanned sharply.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: uploads.
• ZIP: not splittable and still full scans.
• Glacier IR: storage class.

Key takeaway: Athena cost → columnar + partitions.

stem: A data lake stores 800 TB of objects with unpredictable and changing access patterns. Some objects are unused for months and then suddenly accessed heavily. Retrieval must remain in milliseconds without retrieval fees. Which storage class minimizes cost?

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
S3 Standard.
S3 Standard-IA.
S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically as access changes, with no retrieval fees for its automatic tiers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard: overpays for cold data.
• Standard-IA: retrieval fees when data gets hot.
• Deep Archive: slow retrieval.

Key takeaway: unpredictable access → Intelligent-Tiering.

stem: A company has steady compute spend across EC2 in two Regions, Fargate tasks, and Lambda functions. It expects to change instance families and Regions over the next three years. Which purchase option saves the most while keeping this flexibility?

choices.text: EC2 Instance Savings Plans.
Compute Savings Plans.
Spot Instances for all workloads.
Standard Reserved Instances for the current instance types.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute Savings Plans cover EC2 in any Region and family, Fargate, and Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 Instance SPs: tied to family and Region.
• Spot for all: not suitable for all workloads.
• Standard RIs: tied to current types.

Key takeaway: mixed compute with changes → Compute Savings Plans.

stem: A nightly batch rendering job is fault-tolerant and checkpoints progress. The team wants the lowest cost while minimizing interruptions. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: Spot Instances of one type in one AZ with the lowest-price strategy.
On-Demand Instances of a single, well-tested instance type.
Dedicated Hosts purchased for three years.
Diversified Spot with price-capacity-optimized allocation.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spot across diverse instance types and AZs with price-capacity-optimized allocation gives low cost with fewer interruptions for checkpointed jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One type, one AZ, lowest-price: interruption-prone.
• On-Demand: costly.
• Dedicated Hosts: costly.

Key takeaway: diversify Spot capacity.

stem: A website serves large static images and videos directly from S3 to global users, and data transfer out charges are growing. Which change reduces cost and improves performance?

choices.text: Move the content to EBS volumes on EC2 web servers in each Region.
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in every Region.
Serve it through CloudFront with OAC.
Enable S3 Requester Pays for all website visitors.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront with origin access control serves content from the edge, cutting latency and transfer costs, and keeps the bucket private.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS on EC2: costly and complex.
• CRR everywhere: storage costs.
• Requester Pays: unsuitable for public visitors.

Key takeaway: global static content → CloudFront + OAC.

stem: A DynamoDB table has a steady, predictable workload of about 5,000 writes per second around the clock that will continue for at least a year. Which capacity choice is MOST cost-effective?

choices.text: On-demand capacity mode for the table.
Provisioned capacity set to 50,000 writes per second to avoid throttling.
Provisioned capacity with auto scaling and reserved capacity.
On-demand capacity mode with DAX in front of the table.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A steady, long-term workload is cheapest on provisioned capacity with auto scaling for variation and reserved capacity for the baseline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-demand: costs more for steady load.
• 10× overprovisioning: waste.
• On-demand with DAX: doesn't lower write cost.

Key takeaway: steady DynamoDB load → provisioned + reserved capacity.

stem: A web application on EC2 needs to upload files to one specific S3 bucket. What is the most secure way to grant access?

choices.text: A bucket policy that allows public write access so the application can upload files
An IAM user's access keys stored in the application's configuration file on the instance
An IAM role attached to the instance with a policy allowing PutObject on that bucket only
The root user's access keys set as environment variables on each application server

explanation:
Why this is correct:
