Instance roles provide temporary credentials, and a scoped policy grants only the needed action on the specific bucket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A bucket policy that allows public write…: Public write is insecure.
• An IAM user's access keys stored in the…: Stored long-term keys can leak.
• The root user's access keys set as…: Root credentials must never be used for applications.

Key takeaway: Use IAM roles with least-privilege policies for workloads.

stem: A mobile app must let users upload photos directly to S3 without routing files through backend servers, and without embedding AWS credentials in the app. Which solution fits?

choices.text: Share the root account password with the mobile development team
Embed an IAM user's access keys in the mobile application package
Generate short-lived presigned URLs from the backend for each upload
Make the bucket publicly writable so any user can upload directly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Presigned URLs grant time-limited permission for a specific upload without exposing credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Share the root account password with the…: Root credentials must never be shared.
• Embed an IAM user's access keys in the…: Embedded keys can be extracted.
• Make the bucket publicly writable so any…: Public write allows abuse.

Key takeaway: Direct client uploads → presigned URLs.

stem: A company wants its employees to sign in to AWS accounts using existing corporate identities from its identity provider. Which service fits?

choices.text: IAM users created manually for every employee in every one of the company's accounts
A shared IAM user whose password is given to all employees
AWS IAM Identity Center federated with the corporate identity provider
Amazon Cognito identity pools for employee console access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center federates with corporate identity providers for single sign-on to AWS accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM users created manually for every…: Manual users are hard to manage and duplicate identities.
• A shared IAM user whose password is given to…: Shared users remove accountability.
• Amazon Cognito identity pools for employee…: Cognito targets application end users.

Key takeaway: Workforce federation → IAM Identity Center.

stem: Users of a web application must sign up, sign in, and use social logins, and the app then needs temporary AWS credentials to access S3. Which combination fits?

choices.text: IAM users created for every application user, each with an individual password
A custom user table in RDS with passwords stored in plaintext
One shared IAM role assumed by the app with no user identity
Cognito user pools for authentication and identity pools for AWS credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
User pools handle sign-up and sign-in (including social), and identity pools exchange tokens for temporary AWS credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM users created for every application…: IAM users do not scale to app users.
• A custom user table in RDS with passwords…: Plaintext passwords are insecure.
• One shared IAM role assumed by the app with…: No per-user identity prevents scoped access.

Key takeaway: App users and AWS credentials → Cognito user pools plus identity pools.

stem: A company must require MFA for all IAM users who access the AWS console. Which approach enforces this?

choices.text: A CloudWatch dashboard showing which users have MFA devices assigned
A bucket policy on every S3 bucket that requires users to use MFA
An IAM policy that denies actions when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false
An email reminding users to enable MFA on their accounts each month

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A deny statement conditioned on MFA presence blocks actions for sessions without MFA.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A CloudWatch dashboard showing which users…: Dashboards do not enforce.
• A bucket policy on every S3 bucket that…: Bucket policies do not cover all actions.
• An email reminding users to enable MFA on…: Reminders do not enforce.

Key takeaway: Enforce MFA with IAM condition keys.

stem: An application in Account A needs to read objects from an S3 bucket in Account B. Which approach is most secure?

choices.text: Copying all objects nightly from Account B to a bucket in Account A
Making the bucket in Account B publicly readable so the application in Account A can read it
Sharing an IAM user's access keys from Account B with Account A
A role in Account B that Account A's role can assume, with read access to the bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account role assumption grants temporary, scoped access without sharing long-term credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copying all objects nightly from Account B…: Copying duplicates data and adds delay.
• Making the bucket in Account B publicly…: Public access exposes data.
• Sharing an IAM user's access keys from…: Shared keys are long-term credentials.

Key takeaway: Cross-account access → role assumption.

stem: A web tier in public subnets and an application tier in private subnets must be isolated so only the web tier can reach the application tier on port 8080. Which control fits?

choices.text: Public IP addresses on the application instances with a firewall script
A route table entry that sends all application tier traffic to the VPC's internet gateway
An application tier security group that allows 8080 only from the web tier security group
A network ACL that allows all traffic between every subnet in the VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups can reference other security groups, allowing traffic only from the web tier.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IP addresses on the application…: Public IPs expose the tier.
• A route table entry that sends all…: An IGW route makes the tier public.
• A network ACL that allows all traffic…: Allowing all traffic removes isolation.

Key takeaway: Reference security groups to control tier-to-tier traffic.

stem: A public web application needs protection against SQL injection and cross-site scripting at the edge. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Shield Standard enabled on the account by default
Security groups with inbound rules for port 443 only
Network ACLs that block traffic from unknown networks
AWS WAF on CloudFront or the ALB with managed rule groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks attacks such as SQL injection and XSS using managed rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Shield Standard enabled on the account…: Shield Standard protects against network DDoS, not web exploits.
• Security groups with inbound rules for port…: Security groups cannot inspect requests.
• Network ACLs that block traffic from unknown…: NACLs filter IP and port only.

Key takeaway: Web exploits → AWS WAF.

stem: EC2 instances in private subnets need to call Amazon DynamoDB without internet access. Which solution fits?

choices.text: Public IP addresses on the instances with a security group
A NAT gateway in a public subnet for all DynamoDB traffic
An internet gateway attached to the private subnets directly
A DynamoDB gateway VPC endpoint added to the private route tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints provide private access to DynamoDB (and S3) without internet or NAT.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IP addresses on the instances with a…: Public IPs expose instances.
• A NAT gateway in a public subnet for all…: NAT sends traffic over the internet and costs more.
• An internet gateway attached to the private…: IGW routes make subnets public.

Key takeaway: Private DynamoDB or S3 access → gateway endpoints.

stem: A company must protect a critical public application from large DDoS attacks and get access to AWS DDoS experts during attacks. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Shield Advanced
AWS Shield Standard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS protection and access to the Shield Response Team.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.
• Amazon GuardDuty: GuardDuty detects threats but does not mitigate DDoS.
• AWS Shield Standard: Shield Standard provides baseline protection without expert access.

Key takeaway: Advanced DDoS protection with expert support → Shield Advanced.

stem: A company wants to connect its on-premises network to a VPC quickly over encrypted tunnels using the internet. Which option fits?

choices.text: VPC peering links
AWS Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Direct Connect
An internet gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN creates IPsec tunnels over the internet and can be set up quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering links: Peering connects VPCs.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect takes longer to provision and is not encrypted by default.
• An internet gateway: IGWs provide internet access, not private tunnels.

Key takeaway: Quick encrypted hybrid link → Site-to-Site VPN.

stem: A company must encrypt S3 data with keys it manages and see every use of the keys in audit logs. Which option fits?

choices.text: S3 Object Lock in governance mode
SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys
No encryption with bucket versioning
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key gives control over the key and logs key usage in CloudTrail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Object Lock in governance mode: Object Lock prevents deletion, not encryption.
• SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 with no per-use audit of a customer key.
• No encryption with bucket versioning: Versioning is not encryption.

Key takeaway: Controlled, auditable S3 encryption → SSE-KMS with a CMK.

stem: A company must keep financial records in S3 unchangeable for seven years, even by the root user. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: S3 Versioning with MFA Delete enabled on the bucket by the root user
An IAM policy denying delete actions to all users
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention period
S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a legal hold

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compliance mode prevents anyone, including root, from deleting or overwriting objects during retention.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Versioning with MFA Delete enabled on the…: Versioning with MFA Delete can still be changed by privileged users.
• An IAM policy denying delete actions to all…: IAM policies do not bind the root user.
• S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a…: Governance mode can be bypassed with special permissions.

Key takeaway: Immutable records even for root → Object Lock compliance mode.

stem: An RDS database must encrypt data at rest. The database already exists unencrypted. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Enable encryption in place from the RDS console settings
Modify the instance class to a type that encrypts by default
Snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption, and restore from it
Enable Multi-AZ, which automatically encrypts the storage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Encryption cannot be enabled on an existing unencrypted instance; restoring from an encrypted snapshot copy creates an encrypted instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable encryption in place from the RDS…: In-place encryption is not supported.
• Modify the instance class to a type that…: Instance class does not encrypt.
• Enable Multi-AZ, which automatically…: Multi-AZ does not encrypt.

Key takeaway: Encrypt existing RDS via encrypted snapshot copy.

stem: A company needs TLS certificates for its CloudFront distribution and ALB that renew automatically at no extra cost. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Secrets Manager storing certificate text
Self-signed certificates on each web server
Certificates uploaded to S3 buckets manually
AWS Certificate Manager public certificates

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM provides free public certificates for integrated services and renews them automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Secrets Manager storing certificate text: Secrets Manager does not issue public certificates.
• Self-signed certificates on each web server: Self-signed certificates are not trusted.
• Certificates uploaded to S3 buckets manually: Manual uploads do not renew.

Key takeaway: Auto-renewing TLS for AWS services → ACM.

stem: A company must discover and classify personal data stored across hundreds of S3 buckets. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config
Amazon Macie
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Shield

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data such as PII in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config: Config tracks configurations.
• Amazon GuardDuty: GuardDuty detects threats.
• AWS Shield: Shield protects against DDoS.

Key takeaway: Find PII in S3 → Macie.

stem: A company wants to prevent any account in its organization from disabling CloudTrail or leaving the organization. Which TWO steps are needed? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enable S3 versioning on the CloudTrail bucket
Create IAM users with restricted permissions
Enable MFA on each account's root user only
Attach an SCP that denies those actions
Use AWS Organizations to manage all accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs within AWS Organizations set guardrails that account administrators cannot override.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable S3 versioning on the CloudTrail bucket: Versioning protects log objects but does not prevent disabling the trail.
• Create IAM users with restricted permissions: Account admins can change IAM users.
• Enable MFA on each account's root user only: MFA does not prevent actions by authenticated admins.

Key takeaway: Organization guardrails → SCPs.

stem: Which TWO measures reduce the attack surface of EC2 instances in a web architecture? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Assign public IPs to every instance for easier access
Place instances in private subnets behind a load balancer
Share one SSH key among all engineers for convenience
Allow all inbound traffic in security groups for testing
Use Session Manager instead of opening SSH to the internet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private placement and keyless, portless administrative access reduce exposure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Assign public IPs to every instance for…: Public IPs expose instances.
• Share one SSH key among all engineers for…: Shared keys remove accountability.
• Allow all inbound traffic in security groups…: Open security groups invite attacks.

Key takeaway: Keep instances private and avoid open SSH.

stem: Which TWO actions protect data in transit between clients and an application behind an ALB? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Allowing only port 80 on the ALB listener
Storing the private key in EC2 user data
An HTTPS listener using an ACM certificate
Disabling TLS to reduce connection latency
An HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect on the listener

explanation:
Why this is correct:
HTTPS listeners encrypt traffic, and redirects ensure clients use HTTPS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allowing only port 80 on the ALB listener: Port 80 is unencrypted.
• Storing the private key in EC2 user data: Keys in user data are insecure.
• Disabling TLS to reduce connection latency: Disabling TLS exposes data.

Key takeaway: Enforce HTTPS at the load balancer.

stem: A developer accidentally committed an IAM user's access key to a public repository. What should be done first?

choices.text: Change the IAM user's console password and keep the same key
Add MFA to the IAM user and continue using the exposed key
Deactivate and rotate the exposed key, then review CloudTrail for misuse
Delete the repository and assume the key was not seen by anyone during the exposure

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Exposed keys must be disabled immediately, replaced, and their use investigated.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Change the IAM user's console password and…: Password changes do not revoke access keys.
• Add MFA to the IAM user and continue using…: MFA does not protect API keys already exposed.
• Delete the repository and assume the key was…: Deleting the repository does not revoke the key.

Key takeaway: Revoke exposed keys immediately and investigate.

stem: An order service and a shipping service are tightly coupled; when shipping is slow, orders fail. Which change decouples them?

choices.text: Merge both services into one application with a shared database
Increase the timeout of synchronous calls from orders to shipping
Run both services on the same EC2 instance to reduce network hops
Send order events to an SQS queue that the shipping service consumes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A queue buffers work between services so a slow consumer does not cause producer failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Merge both services into one application…: Merging increases coupling.
• Increase the timeout of synchronous calls…: Longer timeouts still tie orders to shipping's availability.
• Run both services on the same EC2 instance…: Co-locating adds a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: Decouple services with queues.

stem: One event from an order service must be delivered to billing, inventory, and analytics services, each processing at its own pace. Which pattern fits?

choices.text: One SQS queue polled by all three services at the same time
An SNS topic with an SQS queue subscribed for each service
A shared database table that all three services poll
Direct HTTP calls from the order service to each service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SNS fan-out to per-service SQS queues delivers each event to every consumer with independent buffering.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One SQS queue polled by all three services…: One queue delivers each message to only one consumer.
• A shared database table that all three…: Polling a table is inefficient and couples services.
• Direct HTTP calls from the order service to…: Direct calls couple services.

Key takeaway: Fan out events with SNS to SQS queues.

stem: A stateless web application's traffic varies widely during the day. The company wants capacity to adjust automatically. Which solution fits?

choices.text: A Lambda function invoked once per hour on a schedule
An Auto Scaling group with target tracking behind an ALB
A fixed number of instances managed manually by staff
A single large EC2 instance sized for peak demand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Auto Scaling with target tracking adjusts capacity to demand, and an ALB distributes traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A Lambda function invoked once per hour on a…: A scheduled function does not serve web traffic.
• A fixed number of instances managed manually…: Manual management is slow.
• A single large EC2 instance sized for peak…: A single instance is a single point of failure and wastes capacity off-peak.

Key takeaway: Variable traffic → Auto Scaling with target tracking.

stem: A workflow coordinates several Lambda functions with branching, retries, and a wait for manual approval. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Step Functions
Amazon SNS topics
Amazon Kinesis
Amazon SQS FIFO

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions orchestrates steps with branching, retries, and callbacks for approvals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SNS topics: SNS publishes messages without orchestration.
• Amazon Kinesis: Kinesis streams data.
• Amazon SQS FIFO: A queue does not orchestrate branching workflows.

Key takeaway: Orchestrate multi-step workflows with Step Functions.

stem: A company wants to expose a serverless REST API with request throttling and API keys for partners. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect
Amazon CloudFront
Elastic Load Balancer
Amazon API Gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway provides managed APIs with throttling, API keys, and usage plans.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is private connectivity.
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.
• Elastic Load Balancer: Load balancers do not provide API keys or usage plans.

Key takeaway: Managed APIs with throttling → API Gateway.

stem: Messages must be processed exactly once and in the order sent for each customer account. Which queue configuration fits?

choices.text: SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue
SQS standard queue with long polling enabled on all consumers
SQS FIFO queue with the account ID as the message group ID
SNS standard topic with many subscribers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FIFO queues preserve order within a message group and support exactly-once processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue: A DLQ does not provide ordering.
• SQS standard queue with long polling enabled…: Standard queues do not guarantee order.
• SNS standard topic with many subscribers: Standard SNS does not guarantee order.

Key takeaway: Ordered, exactly-once per key → SQS FIFO with message groups.

stem: A web application runs on EC2 in one Availability Zone. The company wants it to survive an AZ failure. Which change fits?

choices.text: Run instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind an ALB
Take daily AMIs and restore them manually after a failure
Attach an Elastic IP address to the primary instance
Move the instances to a larger instance type that stays in the same Availability Zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spreading instances across AZs behind a load balancer keeps the application available if one AZ fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Take daily AMIs and restore them manually…: Manual restores cause downtime.
• Attach an Elastic IP address to the primary…: Elastic IPs do not add redundancy.
• Move the instances to a larger instance type…: A larger instance in one AZ still fails with the AZ.

Key takeaway: Survive AZ failures with multi-AZ Auto Scaling.

stem: A company's database must fail over automatically within about a minute if its primary fails, with no data loss. Which option fits?

choices.text: RDS single instance with backups
Manual snapshots every hour
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment
A read replica in the same AZ

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication to a standby and fails over automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RDS single instance with backups: Restoring backups takes longer and may lose data.
• Manual snapshots every hour: Hourly snapshots lose data.
• A read replica in the same AZ: A same-AZ replica does not fail over automatically and replicates asynchronously.

Key takeaway: Automatic database failover without data loss → Multi-AZ.

stem: A static website must remain available if the primary S3 bucket's Region has an outage. Which design fits?

choices.text: Store the website on a single EC2 instance instead
Enable versioning and MFA Delete on the bucket in the single Region only
Use S3 One Zone-IA storage for all website files
Replicate the bucket to another Region and use CloudFront origin failover

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CRR plus CloudFront origin failover serves content from a second Region if the primary fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Store the website on a single EC2 instance…: One instance is a single point of failure.
• Enable versioning and MFA Delete on the…: Versioning does not add Regional redundancy.
• Use S3 One Zone-IA storage for all website files: One Zone-IA reduces resilience.

Key takeaway: Regional resilience for static sites → CRR plus origin failover.

stem: A company needs its DNS to route users to a healthy Region if the primary Region fails. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Route 53 simple routing with one record
Route 53 failover routing with health checks
Route 53 weighted routing with no checks
A static IP hard-coded in the client apps

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Failover routing uses health checks to direct traffic to the secondary Region when the primary is unhealthy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 simple routing with one record: Simple routing has no failover.
• Route 53 weighted routing with no checks: Weighted routing without health checks keeps sending traffic to failed endpoints.
• A static IP hard-coded in the client apps: Hard-coded IPs cannot fail over.

Key takeaway: DNS-based Regional failover → failover routing.

stem: Private instances in three AZs use a single NAT gateway. Which change improves availability?

choices.text: Move all instances into the AZ that hosts the NAT gateway
Create a NAT gateway in each AZ and route each AZ to its own
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance of a larger size
Add a second internet gateway to the VPC for redundancy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NAT gateways are zonal; one per AZ avoids losing outbound access when an AZ fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move all instances into the AZ that hosts…: Consolidating into one AZ reduces availability.
• Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance…: A single NAT instance is still a single point of failure.
• Add a second internet gateway to the VPC for…: A VPC can have only one internet gateway.

Key takeaway: Deploy one NAT gateway per AZ.

stem: An application needs shared file storage for Linux instances across multiple AZs that remains available if one AZ fails. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon EBS snapshots
Amazon EBS volume on one instance
Amazon EFS Regional file system
EC2 instance store volumes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS Regional file systems store data across multiple AZs and can be mounted from each AZ.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EBS snapshots: Snapshots are backups, not shared storage.
• Amazon EBS volume on one instance: EBS volumes are single-AZ.
• EC2 instance store volumes: Instance store is ephemeral and local.

Key takeaway: Multi-AZ shared Linux storage → EFS.

stem: A company needs to recover a deleted DynamoDB item that was removed by mistake two days ago. Which feature allows this?

choices.text: Point-in-time recovery on the table
Time to live on table items
DynamoDB Streams on the table
DynamoDB Accelerator in front

explanation:
Why this is correct:
PITR allows restoring the table to any point within the last 35 days.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Time to live on table items: TTL deletes items.
• DynamoDB Streams on the table: Streams capture recent changes but are not a restore feature.
• DynamoDB Accelerator in front: DAX caches reads.

Key takeaway: Restore DynamoDB to a past point → PITR.

stem: A company needs an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes for its EC2-based application in a second Region at low ongoing cost. Which service fits?

choices.text: AMIs copied once a month
S3 Cross-Region Replication
Daily AWS Backup plans only
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates servers at low cost and launches recovery instances in minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AMIs copied once a month: Monthly AMIs miss both objectives.
• S3 Cross-Region Replication: CRR replicates S3 objects, not servers.
• Daily AWS Backup plans only: Daily backups miss a seconds RPO.

Key takeaway: Low-cost continuous server replication → Elastic Disaster Recovery.

stem: Which TWO services help build loosely coupled architectures? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect
Amazon EBS
Amazon EC2 Instance Store
Amazon EventBridge
Amazon SQS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Queues and event buses let components communicate asynchronously without direct dependencies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is network connectivity.
• Amazon EBS: EBS is block storage.
• Amazon EC2 Instance Store: Instance store is local storage.

Key takeaway: Loose coupling → queues and event buses.

stem: Which TWO actions improve the availability of an application backed by Amazon Aurora? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Disable automated backups to reduce write overhead
Use the cluster endpoint so failover is transparent
Connect directly to the writer instance's IP address
Place all replicas in the writer's Availability Zone
Add Aurora Replicas in other Availability Zones

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Replicas in other AZs enable failover, and the cluster endpoint follows the current writer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable automated backups to reduce write…: Disabling backups harms recovery.
• Connect directly to the writer instance's IP…: Hard-coded IPs break after failover.
• Place all replicas in the writer's…: Same-AZ replicas fail with the AZ.

Key takeaway: Cross-AZ replicas plus cluster endpoints for Aurora availability.

stem: A company wants to process uploaded images asynchronously and automatically when they arrive in S3, without managing servers. Which design fits?

choices.text: A cron job on-premises that downloads new files
A Kinesis stream that users write images into
S3 event notifications invoking a Lambda function
An EC2 instance polling the bucket every minute

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 events can trigger Lambda directly, processing each new object without servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A cron job on-premises that downloads new files: On-premises cron is unrelated and slow.
• A Kinesis stream that users write images into: Kinesis is not designed for image file uploads.
• An EC2 instance polling the bucket every minute: Polling wastes resources and adds delay.

Key takeaway: React to S3 uploads with event notifications and Lambda.

stem: A company must back up EC2, EBS, RDS, and EFS on a schedule with centralized retention policies. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Backup
AWS Storage Gateway
AWS DataSync
AWS Snowball

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Backup provides centralized, policy-based backups across many services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Storage Gateway: Storage Gateway connects on-premises storage.
• AWS DataSync: DataSync transfers files.
• AWS Snowball: Snowball moves data offline.

Key takeaway: Centralized multi-service backups → AWS Backup.

stem: A company runs containers and wants AWS to manage the underlying servers so it only defines tasks and services. Which option fits?

choices.text: Kubernetes on on-premises VMs
Docker on a single EC2 host
Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate runs containers without provisioning or managing servers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Kubernetes on on-premises VMs: On-premises VMs require full management.
• Docker on a single EC2 host: A single host is unmanaged and a single point of failure.
• Amazon ECS on self-managed EC2: EC2 launch type requires managing instances.

Key takeaway: Serverless containers → Fargate.

stem: A company compares pilot light and warm standby DR strategies. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Pilot light runs full production capacity in both Regions at all times
Warm standby keeps only backups with no running resources in the second Region
Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy, recovering faster than pilot light at higher cost
Pilot light always recovers faster than warm standby at a higher cost

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Warm standby keeps a running, scaled-down environment; pilot light keeps only core components, so it is cheaper but slower.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pilot light runs full production capacity in…: That describes active-active.
• Warm standby keeps only backups with no…: That describes backup and restore.
• Pilot light always recovers faster than warm…: Pilot light is generally slower and cheaper.

Key takeaway: Warm standby is faster and costlier than pilot light.

stem: An application needs block storage with consistent high IOPS for a transactional database on EC2. Which EBS volume type fits best?

choices.text: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)
Magnetic previous-generation disks
Cold HDD storage volumes (sc1)
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
io2 volumes deliver consistent, high IOPS for demanding transactional databases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Magnetic previous-generation disks: Magnetic volumes are low-performance legacy storage.
• Cold HDD storage volumes (sc1): sc1 targets infrequent access.
• Throughput Optimized HDD (st1): st1 targets sequential throughput.

Key takeaway: High, consistent IOPS → Provisioned IOPS SSD.

stem: A big data job reads large files sequentially from block storage at high throughput, and cost matters. Which EBS type fits?

choices.text: Cold HDD storage (sc1)
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
General Purpose SSD (gp3)
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
st1 is designed for frequently accessed, throughput-intensive sequential workloads at low cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cold HDD storage (sc1): sc1 is for infrequently accessed data.
• General Purpose SSD (gp3): gp3 is general purpose and costs more per GB for this use.
• Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2): io2 is costly and optimized for IOPS.

Key takeaway: Sequential throughput at low cost → st1.

stem: Users worldwide upload large files to a single S3 bucket and experience slow uploads. Which feature helps?

choices.text: S3 Requester Pays mode
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Object Lock settings
S3 Intelligent-Tiering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through edge locations over the AWS network, speeding long-distance transfers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Requester Pays mode: Requester Pays shifts request costs.
• S3 Object Lock settings: Object Lock prevents deletion.
• S3 Intelligent-Tiering: Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage cost.

Key takeaway: Faster long-distance uploads → Transfer Acceleration.

stem: Large files uploaded to S3 often fail midway over unreliable networks. Which approach improves reliability and speed?

choices.text: Uploading files one byte at a time in sequence
Compressing files into one larger archive object
Multipart upload with parallel parts and retries
Single PUT requests with longer client timeouts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multipart upload sends parts in parallel and retries only failed parts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Uploading files one byte at a time in sequence: Byte-by-byte uploads are impractical.
• Compressing files into one larger archive object: Larger objects increase failure impact.
• Single PUT requests with longer client timeouts: Single PUTs restart entirely on failure.

Key takeaway: Large uploads → multipart upload.

stem: A workload needs high compute performance for video encoding with many CPU cores. Which EC2 instance family fits?

choices.text: Compute optimized instances such as C family
Memory optimized instances such as R family
Burstable instances such as the T family
Storage optimized instances such as I family

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute optimized instances offer high CPU performance for encoding and batch processing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Memory optimized instances such as R family: Memory optimized suits large in-memory data.
• Burstable instances such as the T family: Burstable instances throttle under sustained load.
• Storage optimized instances such as I family: Storage optimized suits high local I/O.

Key takeaway: CPU-heavy workloads → compute optimized instances.

stem: An in-memory analytics application needs hundreds of GiB of RAM per instance. Which instance family fits?

choices.text: Burstable general-purpose instances such as T family
Compute optimized instances such as the C family
Accelerated computing instances with GPUs only
Memory optimized instances such as R or X families

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Memory optimized instances provide high memory-to-CPU ratios for in-memory workloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Burstable general-purpose instances such as…: Burstable instances are for variable low workloads.
• Compute optimized instances such as the C family: Compute optimized has less memory per vCPU.
• Accelerated computing instances with GPUs only: GPUs are for parallel compute, not memory capacity.

Key takeaway: Large in-memory workloads → memory optimized instances.

stem: An application runs short, event-driven tasks for a few seconds each, triggered by S3 uploads. Which compute option fits best?

choices.text: Amazon EMR
AWS Lambda
Amazon EC2
AWS Batch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda runs short, event-driven code without servers and scales per event.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EMR: EMR is for big data clusters.
• Amazon EC2: EC2 requires managing servers.
• AWS Batch: Batch targets longer batch jobs.

Key takeaway: Short event-driven tasks → Lambda.

stem: A read-heavy application's RDS database is overloaded by read queries. Which change improves performance?

choices.text: Enable Multi-AZ and send reads to the standby instance
Increase the backup retention period of the database
Add RDS read replicas and route read queries to them
Enable storage auto scaling to add more disk space

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas offload read traffic from the primary database.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable Multi-AZ and send reads to the…: The Multi-AZ instance standby does not serve reads.
• Increase the backup retention period of the…: Backup retention does not affect performance.
• Enable storage auto scaling to add more disk…: Storage scaling does not reduce read load.

Key takeaway: Scale reads with read replicas.

stem: A session store needs sub-millisecond latency and must handle millions of reads per second. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon RDS MySQL
Amazon Redshift
Amazon S3 Standard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ElastiCache provides in-memory storage with sub-millisecond latency at high throughput.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon RDS MySQL: RDS has higher latency.
• Amazon Redshift: Redshift is for analytics.
• Amazon S3 Standard: S3 has higher latency.

Key takeaway: Sub-millisecond key-value access → ElastiCache.

stem: A serverless application's Lambda functions open many connections to an RDS database and exhaust connection limits. Which service helps?

choices.text: Amazon SQS FIFO
Amazon Route 53
Amazon CloudFront
Amazon RDS Proxy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS Proxy pools connections, preventing Lambda bursts from exhausting database connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS FIFO: SQS queues messages.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 provides DNS.
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.

Key takeaway: Pool database connections for Lambda with RDS Proxy.

stem: A gaming application needs a database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale and flexible schemas. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Redshift
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon RDS for MySQL
Amazon Athena

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB provides consistent single-digit millisecond performance at any scale with flexible schemas.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Redshift: Redshift is analytical.
• Amazon RDS for MySQL: RDS scales vertically with fixed schemas.
• Amazon Athena: Athena queries data in S3.

Key takeaway: Low latency at any scale → DynamoDB.

stem: A company serves static and dynamic content to global users and wants lower latency. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
AWS Direct Connect
Amazon VPC peering
Amazon CloudFront

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches static content at edge locations and accelerates dynamic content to global users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Site-to-Site VPN: VPN connects networks.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is private connectivity.
• Amazon VPC peering: Peering connects VPCs.

Key takeaway: Global latency → CloudFront.

stem: A multiplayer game uses UDP and needs static IP addresses with fast routing to the nearest healthy Region. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator
Application Load Balancer
Amazon Route 53 simple
Amazon CloudFront

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS network to the nearest healthy endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Application Load Balancer: ALB does not support UDP.
• Amazon Route 53 simple: Simple routing has no health-based routing.
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront focuses on HTTP content.

Key takeaway: UDP plus static IPs globally → Global Accelerator.

stem: An application needs a load balancer that handles millions of TCP connections per second with ultra-low latency and static IPs per AZ. Which option fits?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLB operates at layer 4 with very high performance and supports static IP addresses per AZ.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Application Load Balancer: ALB is layer 7 for HTTP routing.
• Gateway Load Balancer: GWLB is for third-party appliances.
• Classic Load Balancer: Classic is legacy.

Key takeaway: High-performance TCP with static IPs → NLB.

stem: An application needs to route requests to different microservices based on URL paths such as /api and /images. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer with path-based rules
Gateway Load Balancer with GENEVE tunnels
Route 53 weighted records for each service
Network Load Balancer with TCP listeners

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB supports path-based routing to different target groups.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway Load Balancer with GENEVE tunnels: GWLB is for appliances.
• Route 53 weighted records for each service: DNS cannot route by URL path.
• Network Load Balancer with TCP listeners: NLB does not inspect HTTP paths.

Key takeaway: URL path routing → ALB rules.

stem: A company must ingest real-time clickstream data from thousands of sources and process it within seconds. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
AWS Snowball Edge devices
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams ingests and processes streaming data in real time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: RDS is not a streaming ingestion service.
• AWS Snowball Edge devices: Snowball moves data offline.
• Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive: Glacier is archival.

Key takeaway: Real-time streaming ingestion → Kinesis Data Streams.

stem: Streaming data must be delivered to S3 in batches, converted to Parquet, with no code to manage. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SQS standard
Amazon SNS topics
AWS Step Functions
Amazon Data Firehose

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firehose delivers streaming data to destinations such as S3 with batching and format conversion.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS standard: SQS queues messages without delivery to S3.
• Amazon SNS topics: SNS publishes messages.
• AWS Step Functions: Step Functions orchestrates workflows.

Key takeaway: Managed stream delivery to S3 → Data Firehose.

stem: Analysts want to run SQL queries directly on data in S3 without loading it into a database. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon Athena
Amazon RDS
Amazon DynamoDB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena runs serverless SQL queries directly against data in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon ElastiCache: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache.
• Amazon RDS: RDS requires loading data.
• Amazon DynamoDB: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database.

Key takeaway: SQL on S3 → Athena.

stem: Which TWO options reduce latency for a globally distributed read-heavy application backed by Aurora MySQL? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Aurora Global Database with read replicas in other Regions
Moving the database to a single Availability Zone
Disabling query caching on the application layer
A larger writer instance in a single Region only
CloudFront caching for cacheable API responses

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Regional read replicas serve local reads, and CloudFront caches cacheable responses near users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Moving the database to a single Availability…: Single-AZ reduces availability.
• Disabling query caching on the application layer: Disabling caching increases latency.
• A larger writer instance in a single Region only: A larger writer does not reduce distance.

Key takeaway: Serve reads close to users.

stem: A company runs a fleet of Linux EC2 instances that must all read and write the same files concurrently. Which TWO services provide this shared file storage? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon EC2 instance store volumes
Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway
Amazon FSx for Lustre
Amazon EFS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS and FSx for Lustre are shared file systems that many Linux instances can mount concurrently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EC2 instance store volumes: Instance store is local to one instance.
• Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Glacier is archival object storage.
• AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway: Tape Gateway is for backup archives.

Key takeaway: Shared Linux file systems → EFS or FSx for Lustre.

stem: Log files in S3 are accessed often for 30 days, rarely for a year, and then must be kept for seven years for compliance. Which approach minimizes cost?

choices.text: Store the logs on large EBS volumes attached to a dedicated logging instance
Move objects to Glacier Deep Archive on the first day
Lifecycle rules moving objects to Standard-IA, then Glacier Deep Archive
Keep all objects in S3 Standard for the entire seven years

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lifecycle transitions match storage class to access patterns, cutting cost over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Store the logs on large EBS volumes attached…: EBS is costlier and not durable object storage.
• Move objects to Glacier Deep Archive on the…: Deep Archive on day one makes frequent 30-day access slow and costly.
• Keep all objects in S3 Standard for the…: Standard is costly for rarely accessed data.

Key takeaway: Match storage classes to access patterns with lifecycle rules.

stem: A dataset has unpredictable access patterns, and the team does not want to manage lifecycle rules. Which storage class fits?

choices.text: S3 Standard-IA storage
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Glacier Instant tier
S3 One Zone-IA storage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically based on access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Standard-IA storage: Standard-IA charges retrieval fees on unpredictable access.
• S3 Glacier Instant tier: Glacier Instant Retrieval is for rarely accessed data.
• S3 One Zone-IA storage: One Zone-IA reduces resilience and charges retrieval.

Key takeaway: Unknown access patterns → Intelligent-Tiering.

stem: Easily reproducible thumbnail images are accessed infrequently. The company wants the lowest-cost S3 option with millisecond access. Which fits?

choices.text: S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Express One Zone
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Standard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA and suits reproducible, infrequently accessed data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Express One Zone: Express One Zone is optimized for high-performance access, not low cost.
• S3 Glacier Deep Archive: Deep Archive retrieval takes hours.
• S3 Standard: Standard costs more.

Key takeaway: Reproducible, infrequent data → One Zone-IA.

stem: A company runs a steady workload on EC2 24/7 for the next three years, but may change instance families. Which purchase option fits?

choices.text: On-Demand Instances only
Compute Savings Plans
Dedicated Hosts only
Spot Instances only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute Savings Plans discount steady usage while allowing changes in instance family, size, and Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• On-Demand Instances only: On-Demand costs more for steady use.
• Dedicated Hosts only: Dedicated Hosts cost more.
• Spot Instances only: Spot can be interrupted.

Key takeaway: Steady usage with flexibility → Compute Savings Plans.

stem: A fault-tolerant batch job can be interrupted and restarted. Which EC2 option minimizes cost?

choices.text: Dedicated Instances
Reserved Instances
On-Demand Instances
Spot Instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spot Instances offer large discounts for interruption-tolerant workloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated Instances: Dedicated Instances cost more.
• Reserved Instances: Reservations suit steady workloads.
• On-Demand Instances: On-Demand costs more.

Key takeaway: Interruptible work → Spot.

stem: A web application's Auto Scaling group runs at 10% CPU most of the time on large instances. Which change reduces cost most?

choices.text: Add more large instances to spread the load more evenly
Purchase Reserved Instances for the current large instance size
Right-size to smaller instances and keep target tracking scaling
Disable Auto Scaling and keep a fixed fleet of large instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Right-sizing removes wasted capacity, and scaling adjusts capacity to demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add more large instances to spread the load…: More instances increase cost.
• Purchase Reserved Instances for the current…: Reserving oversized instances locks in waste.
• Disable Auto Scaling and keep a fixed fleet…: A fixed fleet wastes money.

Key takeaway: Right-size before committing.

stem: An API receives only a few hundred requests per day with occasional spikes. Which compute option minimizes cost?

choices.text: A dedicated host for the API
An EKS cluster with three nodes
Two EC2 instances running 24/7
AWS Lambda behind API Gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda charges per request and duration, which is cheapest for low, spiky traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A dedicated host for the API: Dedicated hosts are expensive.
• An EKS cluster with three nodes: EKS has fixed costs.
• Two EC2 instances running 24/7: Always-on instances cost more at low volume.

Key takeaway: Low, spiky traffic → serverless.

stem: A development database is used only during business hours. Which change reduces cost?

choices.text: Enable Multi-AZ for the development database
Stop the RDS instance outside business hours on a schedule
Purchase a three-year Reserved Instance for it
Increase the instance size so work finishes faster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stopping unused databases avoids paying for idle compute.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable Multi-AZ for the development database: Multi-AZ doubles cost.
• Purchase a three-year Reserved Instance for it: Reservations pay for idle hours.
• Increase the instance size so work finishes…: Larger instances cost more.

Key takeaway: Stop non-production databases when idle.

stem: A new application has unpredictable, intermittent database usage with long idle periods. Which option minimizes cost?

choices.text: Aurora Serverless v2
Self-managed MySQL on EC2
Provisioned Aurora cluster
RDS with Multi-AZ always on

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with demand, reducing cost for variable usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed MySQL on EC2: Self-managed EC2 costs money when idle and adds management.
• Provisioned Aurora cluster: Provisioned capacity costs money when idle.
• RDS with Multi-AZ always on: Always-on Multi-AZ costs more.

Key takeaway: Variable database load → Aurora Serverless v2.

stem: A DynamoDB table has steady, predictable traffic all day. Which capacity mode is most cost-effective?

choices.text: DAX cluster with no table changes
On-demand capacity for all traffic
Provisioned capacity with auto scaling
Global tables in three Regions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Provisioned capacity is generally cheaper than on-demand for steady, predictable traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DAX cluster with no table changes: DAX adds cost and does not change capacity mode.
• On-demand capacity for all traffic: On-demand costs more for steady traffic.
• Global tables in three Regions: Global tables add cost.

Key takeaway: Steady DynamoDB traffic → provisioned capacity.

stem: EC2 instances in private subnets transfer large amounts of data to S3 through a NAT gateway, and costs are high. Which change reduces cost?

choices.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
Add a second NAT gateway in the AZ
Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint
Use public subnets with public IPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints route S3 traffic privately without NAT data processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration: Transfer Acceleration adds cost.
• Add a second NAT gateway in the AZ: More NAT gateways add cost.
• Use public subnets with public IPs: Public subnets expose instances.

Key takeaway: Avoid NAT charges for S3 with gateway endpoints.

stem: A company serves large video files to users worldwide from EC2 in one Region, and data transfer costs are high. Which change reduces cost?

choices.text: Serve content through CloudFront with caching
Replicate the EC2 video servers to every AWS Region
Increase EC2 network bandwidth
Use larger EBS volumes for videos

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caches content at the edge, reducing origin data transfer and often lowering delivery cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replicate the EC2 video servers to every AWS…: Replicating servers everywhere adds cost.
• Increase EC2 network bandwidth: Bandwidth does not reduce transfer charges.
• Use larger EBS volumes for videos: Volume size does not affect transfer.

Key takeaway: Global content delivery cost → CloudFront.

stem: Two application tiers exchange large volumes of data across Availability Zones, and inter-AZ charges are rising. The workload can tolerate brief failover. What reduces cost?

choices.text: Route traffic between tiers through the internet
Add a NAT gateway between the two tiers
Move one of the tiers to another AWS Region so the traffic is spread more widely
Keep chatty components in the same AZ while retaining a standby elsewhere

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Keeping heavy traffic within one AZ avoids inter-AZ charges while a standby preserves resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route traffic between tiers through the internet: Internet routing adds cost and risk.
• Add a NAT gateway between the two tiers: NAT adds processing charges.
• Move one of the tiers to another AWS Region…: Cross-Region transfer costs more.

Key takeaway: Reduce cross-AZ chatter to cut data transfer costs.

stem: Which TWO actions reduce S3 storage costs for a bucket with many old object versions? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Lifecycle rules to expire noncurrent versions
Enabling Requester Pays on the bucket for all users
Copying all versions to a second bucket for safety
Lifecycle rules to transition noncurrent versions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Expiring or transitioning noncurrent versions reduces the cost of versioned buckets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket: Transfer Acceleration adds cost.
• Enabling Requester Pays on the bucket for…: Requester Pays shifts request costs, not storage.
• Copying all versions to a second bucket for…: Copying doubles storage.

Key takeaway: Manage noncurrent versions with lifecycle rules.

stem: Which TWO tools help identify cost savings in an AWS account? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake
AWS Artifact
Amazon Inspector
AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Compute Optimizer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
