Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS CloudTrail Lake: CloudTrail Lake queries API activity.
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides compliance reports.
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector finds vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: Find savings with Cost Explorer and Compute Optimizer.

stem: An analytics team runs occasional SQL queries on data in S3 and wants to pay only per query. Which approach is most cost-effective?

choices.text: An RDS instance loaded with the data every morning
A provisioned Redshift cluster running continuously
Amazon Athena on compressed, partitioned Parquet data
An EMR cluster running 24/7 for ad hoc queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena charges per data scanned; compressed, partitioned columnar data reduces scanned bytes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An RDS instance loaded with the data every…: Daily loads into RDS are costly and slow.
• A provisioned Redshift cluster running…: Always-on clusters cost money when idle.
• An EMR cluster running 24/7 for ad hoc queries: Always-on EMR is costly.

Key takeaway: Pay-per-query on S3 → Athena with columnar data.

stem: A company's ECS services run on EC2 with low utilization. Which change can reduce cost and management?

choices.text: Use Dedicated Hosts for all of the container instances in the ECS cluster
Move services to Fargate or right-size and bin-pack with capacity providers
Add more EC2 instances to the cluster for extra headroom
Run each container on its own separate large EC2 instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fargate removes idle instance capacity, and capacity providers with bin-packing improve utilization on EC2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use Dedicated Hosts for all of the container…: Dedicated Hosts cost more.
• Add more EC2 instances to the cluster for…: More instances increase cost.
• Run each container on its own separate large…: One container per large instance wastes capacity.

Key takeaway: Improve container cost with Fargate or better bin-packing.

stem: A company needs on-premises applications to use cloud storage for backups with local caching, minimizing on-premises hardware. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Storage Gateway
AWS Direct Connect
Amazon FSx for Lustre
Amazon EBS snapshots

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Storage Gateway provides on-premises access to cloud storage with local caching for backups and file shares.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is networking, not storage.
• Amazon FSx for Lustre: FSx for Lustre is for HPC in AWS.
• Amazon EBS snapshots: EBS snapshots are for EBS volumes.

Key takeaway: Hybrid storage with local cache → Storage Gateway.

stem: A company wants to track and alert on monthly spending per project. Which TWO steps help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Use one account for all projects with no tags
Disable Cost Explorer to reduce reporting costs
Create AWS Budgets filtered by project tags
Remove tags from resources to simplify billing
Activate cost allocation tags for project tags

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Activated cost allocation tags enable project-level cost tracking, and Budgets alert on spending thresholds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use one account for all projects with no tags: No tags prevents tracking.
• Disable Cost Explorer to reduce reporting costs: Disabling Cost Explorer removes visibility.
• Remove tags from resources to simplify billing: Removing tags removes attribution.

Key takeaway: Track project costs with tags and budgets.

stem: A company wants to grant a contractor temporary access to one S3 bucket for two weeks without creating long-term credentials. Which approach fits?

choices.text: An IAM role the contractor can assume with a scoped policy and limited session duration
A bucket policy that allows public read and write access for the two weeks
The company administrator's credentials shared for the two-week project period
An IAM user with access keys that the contractor must promise to delete afterward

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Role assumption provides temporary credentials with scoped permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A bucket policy that allows public read and…: Public access exposes data.
• The company administrator's credentials…: Sharing admin credentials is insecure.
• An IAM user with access keys that the…: Access keys are long-term credentials.

Key takeaway: Temporary access → assumable roles, not users or shared keys.

stem: A company wants to limit the maximum permissions developers can grant to the IAM roles they create. Which feature fits?

choices.text: VPC security group references
S3 bucket access control lists
AWS Budgets with alert actions
IAM permissions boundaries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Permissions boundaries cap the maximum permissions an IAM entity can have.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC security group references: Security groups control network traffic.
• S3 bucket access control lists: ACLs control S3 object access.
• AWS Budgets with alert actions: Budgets control spending.

Key takeaway: Cap delegated permissions with permissions boundaries.

stem: An auditor asks which IAM users have unused access keys and when passwords were last changed. Which feature provides this quickly?

choices.text: The CloudFront usage report
The IAM credential report
The S3 inventory report
The Cost and Usage Report

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The credential report lists users and credential status, including key usage and password age.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The CloudFront usage report: CloudFront reports cover content delivery.
• The S3 inventory report: S3 inventory lists objects.
• The Cost and Usage Report: CUR covers billing.

Key takeaway: Credential status across users → IAM credential report.

stem: A policy allows s3:* on a bucket, but a user still gets Access Denied. The bucket belongs to another account. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The user needs MFA only for console access, not for API calls
The S3 bucket is in a Region that the user's policy does not name
The bucket policy in the owning account does not grant the user access
The user's password has expired and must be reset in the console

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account access requires permission from both the caller's identity policy and the resource owner's bucket policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The user needs MFA only for console access,…: MFA is not implied as the cause.
• The S3 bucket is in a Region that the user's…: S3 permissions do not require naming Regions.
• The user's password has expired and must be…: Password expiry affects console sign-in, not API permissions here.

Key takeaway: Cross-account access needs both identity and resource policy grants.

stem: An application tier must be reachable only from the web tier, and the database only from the application tier. Which design fits?

choices.text: Public subnets for all tiers with security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0
Network ACLs that allow all traffic within the whole VPC CIDR range
One security group shared by all tiers that allows all inbound traffic
Separate security groups per tier, each allowing traffic only from the tier in front

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Chained security groups restrict each tier to traffic from the previous tier.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public subnets for all tiers with security…: Public exposure is insecure.
• Network ACLs that allow all traffic within…: Allowing all VPC traffic removes isolation.
• One security group shared by all tiers that…: One open group removes isolation.

Key takeaway: Chain security groups tier by tier.

stem: A company wants to block traffic from a set of malicious IP addresses to all public subnets quickly. Security groups allow only permit rules. Which control fits?

choices.text: Network ACL deny rules on the public subnets
A security group rule with a deny statement
An IAM policy denying the IP addresses
A Route 53 record pointing to a blackhole

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs support explicit deny rules at the subnet level.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A security group rule with a deny statement: Security groups cannot deny.
• An IAM policy denying the IP addresses: IAM policies do not filter network traffic.
• A Route 53 record pointing to a blackhole: DNS records do not block inbound traffic.

Key takeaway: Explicit network denies → NACLs.

stem: A company wants to inspect and filter traffic leaving its VPC to the internet, allowing only approved domains. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty with default settings
AWS Network Firewall with domain allow lists
Security groups with outbound rules by IP
An internet gateway with a route table only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Firewall supports stateful domain filtering for egress traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon GuardDuty with default settings: GuardDuty detects threats but does not filter traffic.
• Security groups with outbound rules by IP: Security groups filter by IP and port, not domain.
• An internet gateway with a route table only: IGWs route but do not filter.

Key takeaway: Domain-based egress filtering → Network Firewall.

stem: Applications in a VPC must access an internal service in another VPC with an overlapping CIDR. Which option fits?

choices.text: A transit gateway with one route table
VPC peering between the two VPCs
Public internet with IP allow lists
AWS PrivateLink with an endpoint service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
PrivateLink exposes a specific service without routing between VPCs, so overlapping CIDRs are not a problem.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A transit gateway with one route table: Overlapping routes conflict.
• VPC peering between the two VPCs: Peering fails with overlapping CIDRs.
• Public internet with IP allow lists: Public routing is less secure.

Key takeaway: Overlapping CIDRs and one service → PrivateLink.

stem: A company wants continuous threat detection that analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Artifact
Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Inspector
AWS Firewall Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty analyzes these data sources to detect threats continuously.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides compliance documents.
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.
• AWS Firewall Manager: Firewall Manager manages firewall rules.

Key takeaway: Continuous threat detection → GuardDuty.

stem: A company must rotate RDS database credentials automatically and let applications retrieve them securely. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Secrets Manager
AWS Certificate Manager
Amazon Cognito user pools
AWS Resource Access Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager stores and rotates credentials, including native rotation for RDS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Certificate Manager: ACM manages TLS certificates.
• Amazon Cognito user pools: Cognito manages app users.
• AWS Resource Access Manager: RAM shares resources.

Key takeaway: Rotating database credentials → Secrets Manager.

stem: A company needs keys stored in single-tenant hardware security modules it controls, for regulatory reasons. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS KMS keys
AWS Secrets Manager
AWS CloudHSM
Amazon Macie

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudHSM provides dedicated HSMs under the customer's exclusive control.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS KMS keys: Standard KMS keys use multi-tenant HSMs managed by AWS.
• AWS Secrets Manager: Secrets Manager stores secrets.
• Amazon Macie: Macie discovers sensitive data.

Key takeaway: Dedicated HSM control → CloudHSM.

stem: A company requires that all new EBS volumes in an account are encrypted automatically. What should be done?

choices.text: Enable EBS encryption by default in each Region
Ask engineers to select encryption when creating volumes
Use instance store volumes for all workloads
Enable encryption on existing snapshots only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS encryption by default encrypts all new volumes in that Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ask engineers to select encryption when…: Manual selection is error-prone.
• Use instance store volumes for all workloads: Instance store is ephemeral.
• Enable encryption on existing snapshots only: Snapshots do not change new volume defaults.

Key takeaway: Enforce EBS encryption by default.

stem: Data in an S3 bucket must be accessible only through a specific VPC endpoint. Which control enforces this?

choices.text: A NACL on the subnet denying access to all S3 IPs
An IAM user policy denying access from outside the office
A bucket policy denying requests where aws:SourceVpce is not the endpoint
A security group on the bucket allowing only the VPC CIDR

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bucket policies with the aws:SourceVpce condition restrict access to a specific VPC endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A NACL on the subnet denying access to all…: NACLs cannot reliably target S3.
• An IAM user policy denying access from…: User policies do not cover all principals or the network path.
• A security group on the bucket allowing only…: Buckets do not have security groups.

Key takeaway: Lock S3 to a VPC endpoint with bucket policy conditions.

stem: A company wants to prevent objects in an S3 bucket from being made public by ACLs. Which setting fits?

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering setting
S3 Block Public Access settings
S3 Requester Pays setting
S3 Transfer Acceleration setting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Block Public Access overrides ACLs and policies that would grant public access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Intelligent-Tiering setting: Intelligent-Tiering optimizes cost.
• S3 Requester Pays setting: Requester Pays shifts request costs.
• S3 Transfer Acceleration setting: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads.

Key takeaway: Prevent public S3 access with Block Public Access.

stem: Which TWO practices follow the principle of least privilege? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Share one IAM user among the whole team
Use the root user for daily administrative tasks
Give all developers AdministratorAccess by default
Grant only the permissions required for each task
Review and remove unused permissions regularly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least privilege means granting only needed permissions and pruning unused ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Share one IAM user among the whole team: Shared users remove accountability.
• Use the root user for daily administrative tasks: Root should not be used daily.
• Give all developers AdministratorAccess by…: Admin access for all violates least privilege.

Key takeaway: Grant minimal permissions and prune regularly.

stem: Which TWO services help protect a public web application at the edge? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon EBS
Amazon RDS
AWS Batch
Amazon CloudFront
AWS WAF

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront absorbs traffic at the edge, and WAF filters malicious requests.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EBS: EBS is block storage.
• Amazon RDS: RDS is a database.
• AWS Batch: Batch runs batch jobs.

Key takeaway: Edge protection → CloudFront plus WAF.

stem: Which TWO options encrypt data at rest in Amazon S3? (Select TWO)

choices.text: SSE-S3 with S3 managed keys
VPC endpoints for S3
S3 Transfer Acceleration
TLS on client connections
SSE-KMS with KMS keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS encrypt objects at rest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC endpoints for S3: Endpoints provide private network paths.
• S3 Transfer Acceleration: Acceleration speeds transfers.
• TLS on client connections: TLS encrypts in transit.

Key takeaway: At-rest S3 encryption → SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS.

stem: A company wants a central view of security findings and compliance checks across its accounts. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Security Hub
AWS DataSync
Amazon CloudFront

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security Hub aggregates findings and runs security standard checks across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Cost Explorer: Cost Explorer analyzes spending.
• AWS DataSync: DataSync transfers data.
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.

Key takeaway: Centralized security posture → Security Hub.

stem: A company needs employees to access a private web application in a VPC without a VPN, with identity-based access checks for each request. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect
AWS Global Accelerator
AWS Verified Access
Amazon Route 53

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Access provides VPN-less, identity- and device-aware access to private applications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is private connectivity from data centers.
• AWS Global Accelerator: Global Accelerator improves routing, not access control.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 is DNS.

Key takeaway: VPN-less zero-trust app access → Verified Access.

stem: A company must keep a record of every configuration change to its security groups for audits. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue
AWS Config
Amazon Polly
Amazon SQS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Config records configuration history and changes for resources such as security groups.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Glue: Glue integrates data.
• Amazon Polly: Polly synthesizes speech.
• Amazon SQS: SQS queues messages.

Key takeaway: Configuration history → AWS Config.

stem: A company wants to detect IAM roles and S3 buckets that are shared with external accounts. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
AWS Trusted Advisor
IAM Access Analyzer
AWS Batch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Access Analyzer identifies resources shared with principals outside the zone of trust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Detective: Detective investigates findings.
• AWS Trusted Advisor: Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks.
• AWS Batch: Batch runs jobs.

Key takeaway: External sharing detection → Access Analyzer.

stem: An application uses a third-party appliance to inspect traffic and must scale it transparently. Which load balancer fits?

choices.text: Gateway Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway Load Balancer deploys, scales, and manages third-party virtual appliances transparently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Application Load Balancer: ALB is for HTTP applications.
• Network Load Balancer: NLB is for TCP/UDP applications.
• Classic Load Balancer: Classic is legacy.

Key takeaway: Scale inspection appliances with Gateway Load Balancer.

stem: A web application stores user sessions in instance memory, so users are logged out when instances are replaced. Which change fixes this?

choices.text: Enable sticky sessions with no expiration
Use one large instance instead of many
Disable Auto Scaling for the application
Store sessions in ElastiCache or DynamoDB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Externalizing session state lets any instance serve any user and survives instance replacement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enable sticky sessions with no expiration: Sticky sessions still lose state on replacement.
• Use one large instance instead of many: One instance is a single point of failure.
• Disable Auto Scaling for the application: Disabling scaling hurts availability.

Key takeaway: Make web tiers stateless.

stem: A company wants to route events from AWS services and SaaS applications to different targets based on event content. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge
Amazon Kinesis
Amazon SQS FIFO
AWS Batch jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge routes events from AWS services and SaaS partners to targets using content-based rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Kinesis: Kinesis streams data for consumers to process.
• Amazon SQS FIFO: SQS queues messages without content routing rules.
• AWS Batch jobs: Batch runs jobs.

Key takeaway: Content-based event routing → EventBridge.

stem: A queue's consumers process messages slowly during spikes, and the backlog grows. Which change helps most?

choices.text: Reduce the message retention period to one minute
Increase the maximum message size to 2 GB
Scale consumers with Auto Scaling based on queue depth
Delete messages that wait longer than a second

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scaling consumers on queue depth adds capacity when the backlog grows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reduce the message retention period to one…: Short retention loses messages.
• Increase the maximum message size to 2 GB: Message size does not speed processing.
• Delete messages that wait longer than a second: Deleting messages loses data.

Key takeaway: Scale consumers on backlog.

stem: Messages that repeatedly fail processing block a queue. Which feature isolates them?

choices.text: A larger batch size for each receive call
A dead-letter queue with a max receive count
A shorter polling interval for consumers
A longer visibility timeout of twelve hours

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A DLQ moves messages that fail too many times, so processing continues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A larger batch size for each receive call: Batch size does not isolate failures.
• A shorter polling interval for consumers: Polling interval does not isolate failures.
• A longer visibility timeout of twelve hours: Longer visibility delays retries but does not remove failing messages.

Key takeaway: Isolate failing messages with DLQs.

stem: A company wants to test how its application responds to an EC2 instance failure in a controlled way. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor checks
Amazon Inspector
AWS Config rules
AWS Fault Injection Service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fault Injection Service runs controlled experiments such as stopping instances to test resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Trusted Advisor checks: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector finds vulnerabilities.
• AWS Config rules: Config evaluates configurations.

Key takeaway: Test resilience with fault injection.

stem: A global application needs a relational database that serves low-latency reads in multiple Regions and can fail over to another Region quickly. Which option fits?

choices.text: DynamoDB global tables
RDS Multi-AZ in one Region
Amazon Aurora Global Database
RDS snapshots copied weekly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aurora Global Database replicates to secondary Regions for local reads and fast Regional failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB global tables: DynamoDB is not relational.
• RDS Multi-AZ in one Region: Multi-AZ stays within one Region.
• RDS snapshots copied weekly: Weekly snapshots are too slow.

Key takeaway: Multi-Region relational reads and DR → Aurora Global Database.

stem: An application must keep serving users if one of three Availability Zones fails, with no reduction in capacity. How should capacity be planned?

choices.text: Provision enough capacity so the remaining two AZs can handle full load
Place all instances in the AZ with the most available capacity
Provision exactly the capacity needed with all AZs working normally
Rely on Auto Scaling in a single AZ to replace failed instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Static stability means running enough spare capacity so losing one AZ does not reduce service.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Place all instances in the AZ with the most…: Single-AZ placement fails with the AZ.
• Provision exactly the capacity needed with…: Losing an AZ would reduce capacity.
• Rely on Auto Scaling in a single AZ to…: Single-AZ scaling does not survive AZ loss.

Key takeaway: Plan capacity for the loss of one AZ.

stem: Which TWO features protect S3 data against accidental deletion? (Select TWO)

choices.text: S3 Storage Lens
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Select queries
MFA Delete
S3 Versioning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Versioning keeps prior versions, and MFA Delete requires MFA to permanently delete versions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Storage Lens: Storage Lens reports usage.
• S3 Transfer Acceleration: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads.
• S3 Select queries: S3 Select queries objects.

Key takeaway: Protect S3 data with versioning and MFA Delete.

stem: A company needs to run containers on Kubernetes with AWS managing the control plane. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon EMR
Amazon EKS
AWS Batch
Amazon ECS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EMR: EMR runs big data frameworks.
• AWS Batch: Batch runs batch jobs.
• Amazon ECS: ECS is AWS's own orchestrator, not Kubernetes.

Key takeaway: Managed Kubernetes → EKS.

stem: A company must recover an EC2-based application in another Region within hours at the lowest cost. Which strategy fits?

choices.text: Multi-site active-active at full production capacity in both Regions
Warm standby at full production scale in the other Region
Backup and restore with AMIs and snapshots copied to the other Region
Pilot light with all servers running in the other Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Backup and restore is the cheapest approach and fits recovery within hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-site active-active at full production…: Active-active is the most expensive.
• Warm standby at full production scale in the…: Full-scale warm standby is costly.
• Pilot light with all servers running in the…: Running all servers is not pilot light and costs more.

Key takeaway: Hours of RTO at lowest cost → backup and restore.

stem: Which TWO options help an application absorb sudden traffic spikes without dropping requests? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Remove the load balancer to reduce overhead
Buffer requests in an SQS queue
Hard-code a maximum of one worker instance
Disable retries in the client applications
Use Auto Scaling for the processing tier

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Queues buffer bursts, and Auto Scaling adds capacity to work through them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the load balancer to reduce overhead: Removing the load balancer reduces availability.
• Hard-code a maximum of one worker instance: One worker cannot absorb spikes.
• Disable retries in the client applications: Disabling retries drops requests.

Key takeaway: Buffer and scale to absorb spikes.

stem: A company wants its Lambda-based API to keep working if a single Availability Zone fails. What is required?

choices.text: Nothing extra, since Lambda runs across multiple AZs by default
Configure a NAT gateway in a single Availability Zone for all of the functions
Attach an Elastic IP address to each function
Deploy a copy of each function manually in every AZ

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lambda runs functions across multiple AZs in a Region automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Configure a NAT gateway in a single…: A single-AZ NAT gateway would add an AZ dependency for VPC-attached functions.
• Attach an Elastic IP address to each function: Functions do not use Elastic IPs.
• Deploy a copy of each function manually in…: Functions are not deployed per AZ.

Key takeaway: Lambda is multi-AZ by default.

stem: A company uses one EC2 instance as a NAT for private subnets. Which change improves resilience with minimal management?

choices.text: Remove NAT entirely and use public IPs everywhere
Add a second NAT instance with no route changes
Replace it with a larger NAT instance in the same AZ
Replace it with NAT gateways in each Availability Zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed NAT gateways in each AZ remove the single point of failure and maintenance burden.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove NAT entirely and use public IPs…: Public IPs expose instances.
• Add a second NAT instance with no route changes: Without route changes, the second instance is unused.
• Replace it with a larger NAT instance in the…: A larger instance is still a single point of failure.

Key takeaway: Use managed NAT gateways per AZ.

stem: A company wants a managed message broker compatible with existing RabbitMQ clients. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SQS
Amazon SNS
Amazon MQ
Amazon MSK

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon MQ provides managed ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ brokers compatible with existing clients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS: SQS uses its own API.
• Amazon SNS: SNS uses its own API.
• Amazon MSK: MSK is managed Kafka.

Key takeaway: Managed RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ → Amazon MQ.

stem: An application writes files to an EC2 instance store volume and loses them when the instance stops. Which change keeps the data?

choices.text: Use a larger instance type with more storage
Increase the size of the instance store volume
Enable detailed monitoring on the instance
Store the files on EBS, EFS, or S3 instead

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance store is ephemeral; persistent storage such as EBS, EFS, or S3 keeps data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use a larger instance type with more storage: Larger instance store is still ephemeral.
• Increase the size of the instance store volume: Size does not make it persistent.
• Enable detailed monitoring on the instance: Monitoring does not preserve data.

Key takeaway: Use persistent storage for data that must survive stops.

stem: A company wants DNS health checks to route traffic only to healthy endpoints and return multiple healthy IP addresses to clients. Which routing policy fits?

choices.text: Latency routing only
Multivalue answer routing
Geolocation routing
Simple routing policy records

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multivalue answer routing returns several healthy records, each with health checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency routing only: Latency routing returns the lowest-latency record.
• Geolocation routing: Geolocation routes by location.
• Simple routing policy records: Simple routing has no health checks.

Key takeaway: Multiple healthy IPs from DNS → multivalue answer routing.

stem: A company processes large batch jobs that require hundreds of instances and job queues with dependencies. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Batch
Amazon SQS
Amazon SNS
AWS Lambda

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Batch manages job queues and provisions compute for large batch workloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS: SQS queues messages but does not manage compute.
• Amazon SNS: SNS publishes notifications.
• AWS Lambda: Lambda has time limits for long batch jobs.

Key takeaway: Large managed batch processing → AWS Batch.

stem: A company wants recovery points for EBS volumes every hour with automatic cleanup after seven days. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Manual snapshots created each hour by the operations team
EC2 instance store backups with cron jobs
S3 lifecycle rules applied to the EBS volumes
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup policies

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DLM and AWS Backup automate snapshot creation and retention.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual snapshots created each hour by the…: Manual snapshots are error-prone.
• EC2 instance store backups with cron jobs: Instance store is ephemeral.
• S3 lifecycle rules applied to the EBS volumes: S3 lifecycle rules do not apply to EBS volumes.

Key takeaway: Automate EBS snapshot schedules and retention.

stem: A company wants to decouple a monolith gradually by extracting features into microservices behind a single API entry point. Which service helps route requests?

choices.text: AWS DataSync jobs
AWS Snowball Edge
Amazon API Gateway
Amazon S3 buckets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway can route specific paths to new services while others still go to the monolith.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS DataSync jobs: DataSync transfers files.
• AWS Snowball Edge: Snowball moves data offline.
• Amazon S3 buckets: S3 stores objects.

Key takeaway: Route requests during decomposition with API Gateway.

stem: A workload needs low-latency file storage for Windows applications with SMB and Active Directory integration. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon S3 Standard storage class
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EBS gp3 volume on one host
Amazon EFS Standard storage class

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB shares with AD integration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon S3 Standard storage class: S3 is object storage.
• Amazon EBS gp3 volume on one host: An EBS volume is not a shared file system.
• Amazon EFS Standard storage class: EFS uses NFS for Linux.

Key takeaway: Windows file shares → FSx for Windows File Server.

stem: An application needs single-digit millisecond access to frequently accessed S3 data in one Availability Zone with the highest request rates. Which storage class fits?

choices.text: S3 Express One Zone
S3 One Zone-IA
S3 Glacier Instant
S3 Standard-IA

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 Express One Zone provides very low latency and high request rates for frequently accessed data in one AZ.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 One Zone-IA: One Zone-IA is for infrequent access.
• S3 Glacier Instant: Glacier Instant Retrieval is for rarely accessed data.
• S3 Standard-IA: Standard-IA is for infrequent access.

Key takeaway: Ultra-low-latency, high-rate S3 access → S3 Express One Zone.

stem: A machine learning training job needs GPU acceleration. Which EC2 instance category fits?

choices.text: Accelerated computing instances such as P or G families
Burstable instances such as the T family
Storage optimized instances such as the I or D families
Memory optimized instances such as X family

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Accelerated computing instances provide GPUs for ML training and graphics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Burstable instances such as the T family: Burstable instances lack GPUs.
• Storage optimized instances such as the I or…: Storage optimized targets local I/O.
• Memory optimized instances such as X family: Memory optimized targets RAM, not GPUs.

Key takeaway: GPU workloads → accelerated computing instances.

stem: A company wants EC2 instances with the best price-performance for general Linux workloads. Which option often fits?

choices.text: Bare metal instances for all apps
AWS Graviton-based instances
Previous-generation instance types
Dedicated Hosts for every workload

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Graviton-based instances offer strong price-performance for many Linux workloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bare metal instances for all apps: Bare metal is for special needs.
• Previous-generation instance types: Older generations usually have worse price-performance.
• Dedicated Hosts for every workload: Dedicated Hosts cost more.

Key takeaway: Improve price-performance with Graviton instances.

stem: A DynamoDB table receives repeated reads for the same items and needs microsecond latency. Which feature fits?

choices.text: DynamoDB Streams
DynamoDB global tables replication
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
DynamoDB TTL

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond read latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB Streams: Streams capture changes.
• DynamoDB global tables replication: Global tables replicate across Regions.
• DynamoDB TTL: TTL expires items.

Key takeaway: Microsecond DynamoDB reads → DAX.

stem: Which TWO actions reduce read latency for an RDS-backed application? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Reduce the instance size to save cost
Increase the backup retention period
Enable Multi-AZ to use the standby for reads
Cache frequent query results in ElastiCache
Add read replicas for read-heavy queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Read replicas offload reads, and caching serves repeated queries from memory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reduce the instance size to save cost: Smaller instances increase latency.
• Increase the backup retention period: Retention does not affect latency.
• Enable Multi-AZ to use the standby for reads: The Multi-AZ instance standby does not serve reads.

Key takeaway: Offload and cache reads.

stem: A company needs consistent network performance and private connectivity between its data center and AWS for large transfers. Which option fits?

choices.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
Internet gateway
VPC peering
AWS Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity with consistent performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Site-to-Site VPN: VPN runs over the internet with variable performance.
• Internet gateway: IGWs provide internet access.
• VPC peering: Peering connects VPCs.

Key takeaway: Consistent private hybrid bandwidth → Direct Connect.

stem: Instances in a placement group need the lowest network latency for tightly coupled HPC. Which placement strategy fits?

choices.text: No placement group at all
Cluster placement group
Spread placement group
Partition placement group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cluster placement groups place instances close together for low latency and high throughput.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No placement group at all: Default placement does not optimize latency.
• Spread placement group: Spread groups separate instances for resilience.
• Partition placement group: Partition groups separate groups of instances for large distributed systems.

Key takeaway: Low-latency HPC → cluster placement group.

stem: A company wants to transform data in S3 with serverless ETL jobs and a central data catalog. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue
Amazon RDS
AWS Outposts
Amazon EBS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Glue provides serverless ETL and a Data Catalog.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon RDS: RDS is a database.
• AWS Outposts: Outposts extends AWS on premises.
• Amazon EBS: EBS is block storage.

Key takeaway: Serverless ETL and catalog → AWS Glue.

stem: Business users need interactive dashboards on data in Athena and Redshift. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon SQS
Amazon Quick Sight
AWS Glue jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Quick Sight provides BI dashboards on data sources such as Athena and Redshift.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Kinesis Data Streams: Kinesis streams data.
• Amazon SQS: SQS queues messages.
• AWS Glue jobs: Glue transforms data.

Key takeaway: BI dashboards → Quick Sight.

stem: A company needs to move 80 TB of data to AWS within a week over a slow internet link. Which option fits?

choices.text: A Site-to-Site VPN upload
S3 Transfer Acceleration
AWS DataSync over the internet
AWS Snowball Edge devices

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Snowball devices move large data volumes offline faster than slow network links allow.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A Site-to-Site VPN upload: VPN is limited by the link.
• S3 Transfer Acceleration: Transfer Acceleration is still limited by bandwidth.
• AWS DataSync over the internet: DataSync is limited by bandwidth.

Key takeaway: Large transfers over slow links → Snowball.

stem: An application needs to store and serve user-uploaded images at any scale with high durability. Which service fits?

choices.text: Instance store
Amazon S3
Amazon EBS
Amazon EFS One Zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 provides highly durable, scalable object storage for images.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance store: Instance store is ephemeral.
• Amazon EBS: EBS attaches to one instance.
• Amazon EFS One Zone: EFS One Zone has lower durability and higher cost per GB for this use.

Key takeaway: Durable, scalable object storage → S3.

stem: A containerized web service needs to scale tasks automatically based on CPU. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Manual task starts by the operations team
A scheduled Lambda that adds one task daily
ECS Service Auto Scaling with target tracking
A fixed desired count set once at launch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECS Service Auto Scaling adjusts task count based on metrics such as CPU.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual task starts by the operations team: Manual scaling is slow.
• A scheduled Lambda that adds one task daily: Daily additions do not track load.
• A fixed desired count set once at launch: A fixed count cannot follow load.

Key takeaway: Scale containers with Service Auto Scaling.

stem: Backups must be kept for ten years and are almost never retrieved; retrieval within 48 hours is acceptable. Which storage class is cheapest?

choices.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Standard-IA
S3 Intelligent-Tiering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class for rarely accessed data with retrieval in hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: Instant Retrieval costs more for data almost never retrieved.
• S3 Standard-IA: Standard-IA costs more.
• S3 Intelligent-Tiering: Intelligent-Tiering adds monitoring costs and is not as cheap for archival.

Key takeaway: Long-term archives → Glacier Deep Archive.

stem: A company runs a steady fleet of the same EC2 instance family in one Region for three years and wants the largest discount. Which option fits?

choices.text: EC2 Instance Savings Plans or Standard Reserved Instances
Spot Instances for all steady production workloads
Dedicated Hosts purchased on demand for each instance
On-Demand instances with detailed monitoring

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance-family commitments provide the largest discounts for steady, predictable usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Spot Instances for all steady production…: Spot can be interrupted.
• Dedicated Hosts purchased on demand for each…: Dedicated Hosts cost more.
• On-Demand instances with detailed monitoring: On-Demand costs more.

Key takeaway: Steady, fixed-family usage → Instance Savings Plans or Standard RIs.

stem: A company has variable workloads and wants to combine Spot and On-Demand capacity in one Auto Scaling group. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Manual scaling with On-Demand only
A mixed instances policy with capacity rebalancing
A single instance type with Spot only
A launch template that uses Dedicated Hosts only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mixed instances policies combine purchase options and instance types, and capacity rebalancing reduces Spot interruptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual scaling with On-Demand only: Manual On-Demand scaling is costly and slow.
• A single instance type with Spot only: A single Spot type risks interruptions.
• A launch template that uses Dedicated Hosts only: Dedicated Hosts are costly.

Key takeaway: Blend Spot and On-Demand with mixed instances policies.

stem: A read-only reporting database copy is needed only for monthly reports. Which approach minimizes cost?

choices.text: Buy a three-year reserved instance for the monthly reporting copy
Run Multi-AZ for the reporting copy at all times
Keep a large read replica running all month long
Restore a snapshot to a temporary instance monthly, then delete it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A temporary instance created only when needed avoids paying for an idle replica.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Buy a three-year reserved instance for the…: Reservations pay for idle time.
• Run Multi-AZ for the reporting copy at all times: Multi-AZ doubles cost.
• Keep a large read replica running all month long: An always-on replica costs more.

Key takeaway: Create temporary resources for occasional needs.

stem: Which TWO actions reduce data transfer costs for an application? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Send internal traffic over public IP addresses
Route all traffic through NAT gateways
Serve cacheable content through CloudFront
Replicate data across Regions unnecessarily
Use VPC gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints avoid NAT charges, and CloudFront caching reduces origin transfer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Send internal traffic over public IP addresses: Public IP routing can add charges.
• Route all traffic through NAT gateways: NAT adds processing charges.
• Replicate data across Regions unnecessarily: Unnecessary replication adds transfer.

Key takeaway: Cut transfer costs with endpoints and edge caching.

stem: A company runs a data warehouse that is idle most of the day and busy for short periods. Which option minimizes cost?

choices.text: A large RDS instance used for analytics
Amazon Redshift Serverless
A provisioned Redshift cluster at peak size
An always-on EMR cluster for queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Redshift Serverless bills for compute used, avoiding idle costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A large RDS instance used for analytics: RDS is not built for warehousing and costs money when idle.
• A provisioned Redshift cluster at peak size: A peak-sized cluster costs money when idle.
• An always-on EMR cluster for queries: Always-on EMR is costly.

Key takeaway: Intermittent analytics → Redshift Serverless.

stem: A company wants to reduce EBS costs for a volume that needs modest IOPS but was provisioned as io2 with high IOPS. Which change fits?

choices.text: Add more io2 volumes to spread the load
Increase io2 IOPS for future growth needs
Switch to gp3 with IOPS matching actual usage
Move the data to instance store volumes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
gp3 provides configurable IOPS at lower cost for moderate needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Add more io2 volumes to spread the load: More volumes cost more.
• Increase io2 IOPS for future growth needs: More IOPS costs more.
• Move the data to instance store volumes: Instance store is ephemeral.

Key takeaway: Right-size EBS volume types and IOPS.

stem: A company wants to know which EC2 instances are underutilized and how much it could save. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail
Amazon Inspector scans
AWS Artifact
AWS Compute Optimizer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization and recommends right-sized instances with savings estimates.

Why the other options are wrong:

• Amazon Inspector scans: Inspector finds vulnerabilities.
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides compliance reports.

stem: A company transfers large amounts of data from EC2 to the internet in a single Region and wants lower transfer costs for downloads. Which option fits?

choices.text: Deliver downloads through CloudFront
Add more Elastic IP addresses
Use larger EC2 instance types
Move data to EBS io2 volumes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront caching and edge delivery reduce origin egress and often lower costs.

Why the other options are wrong:

• Use larger EC2 instance types: Instance size does not reduce transfer costs.
• Move data to EBS io2 volumes: Storage type does not affect egress.

stem: A product catalog changes rarely but is read millions of times per day from a relational database. Which approach improves performance most cost-effectively?

choices.text: Move the catalog into S3 Glacier and restore items when users request them
Cache catalog queries in ElastiCache using a lazy-loading pattern with a TTL
Scale the database vertically to the largest available instance class size
Add Multi-AZ so the standby instance can serve half of the catalog reads

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Caching rarely changing, frequently read data offloads the database and lowers latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move the catalog into S3 Glacier and restore…: Glacier retrieval is far too slow.
• Scale the database vertically to the largest…: Scaling up is costly and still hits the database for every read.
• Add Multi-AZ so the standby instance can…: The standby does not serve reads.

Key takeaway: Cache hot, rarely changing data.

stem: A security team must guarantee that no principal outside the company's AWS organization can read data from any S3 bucket in its 60 member accounts, even if a developer later writes a bucket policy that grants access to an external account. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST ongoing effort?

choices.text: Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the organization root that denies S3 access when aws:PrincipalOrgID does not match the organization
Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level in every member account and turn on IAM Access Analyzer for all of those accounts
Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the organization root that denies S3 access when aws:PrincipalOrgID does not match the organization
Deploy an AWS Config rule that detects external principals in bucket policies and triggers a Lambda function to remove the offending statements

explanation:
## Two kinds of organization guardrails
AWS Organizations offers two authorization policy types that set a ceiling on permissions but never grant anything:
- **Service control policies (SCPs)** apply to IAM users and roles *in* member accounts. They answer "what may my principals do?"
- **Resource control policies (RCPs)** apply to resources *in* member accounts, such as S3 buckets, KMS keys, SQS queues and Secrets Manager secrets. They answer "what may anyone do to my resources?"
## Building a data perimeter
A typical RCP statement denies `s3:*` on all resources when the caller's `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is not `o-exampleorgid`, with an exception such as `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` so AWS services acting on your behalf keep working.
Because the RCP is evaluated together with the bucket policy, an explicit deny in the RCP wins over any allow a developer writes later. Example: a bucket policy grants `s3:GetObject` to account `999988887777`; with the RCP in place the request from that account is still denied.
RCPs do not apply to resources in the management account or to actions taken by service-linked roles, so keep workload data in member accounts.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Resource control policy (correct):** an RCP sets the maximum permissions on the resources in member accounts, whoever the caller is. A deny for callers whose `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is not the organization therefore blocks external accounts even when a bucket policy grants them access, and it is set once at the root.
- ✗ **B. Block Public Access plus Access Analyzer:** Block Public Access stops public (anonymous or everyone) grants, but a grant to one specific external account ID is not public. Access Analyzer only reports such access after the fact; it does not prevent it.
- ✗ **C. Service control policy:** SCPs only limit principals that belong to the organization's own accounts. A role in an external account is not governed by the company's SCPs, so a permissive bucket policy would still let it in.
- ✗ **D. Config rule with Lambda remediation:** this is detective and reactive. Between the policy change and the remediation run the external account can read data, and the custom rule and function must be maintained.

## Key idea
SCPs cap what your own principals can do; RCPs cap what anyone can do to your resources, which is how you build an organization-wide data perimeter.

stem: A company with data residency rules must prevent every IAM principal in its workload accounts, including account administrators, from creating resources outside eu-west-1 and eu-central-1. Global services such as IAM, CloudFront, and Route 53 must keep working. What should a solutions architect do?

choices.text: Deploy an AWS Config rule in every Region that marks resources outside the EU as noncompliant and deletes them with an automatic remediation action
Opt out of all other Regions in each account's settings page so those Regions cannot be used, and leave global service endpoints enabled for every principal
Attach an SCP that denies all actions except global services when aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-west-1 or eu-central-1 to the workload OU
Attach a permissions boundary to every IAM user and role in the workload accounts that allows actions only when aws:RequestedRegion is an EU Region

explanation:
## How Region restriction works
Every Regional API call carries the condition key `aws:RequestedRegion`, for example `eu-west-1`. A service control policy (SCP) attached to an organizational unit (OU) can deny calls when that key is not in an approved list.
## The global service exception
Some services, such as IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, Organizations and Support, are global and their API calls are made against `us-east-1`. A plain Region deny would break them, so the statement uses `NotAction` to exclude them:
- `"Effect": "Deny"`, `"NotAction": ["iam:*", "cloudfront:*", "route53:*", ...]`
- `"Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-west-1", "eu-central-1"]}}`
## Why an SCP
SCPs apply to every IAM user and role in the member accounts, including administrators, and they can be changed only from the management account (or a delegated administrator for policy management), never from the member account itself. The root user of a member account is also restricted.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Config rule with deletion:** this detects resources after they already exist outside the EU, which may already violate residency rules, and automatic deletion of workloads is risky. It does not prevent creation.
- ✗ **B. Opt out of Regions:** only opt-in Regions (those launched after March 2019) can be disabled. Default Regions such as us-east-1 or ap-northeast-1 are always enabled and cannot be turned off, so this leaves most Regions open.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** SCP with aws:RequestedRegion: a deny statement using `NotAction` for the global services and a `StringNotEquals` condition on `aws:RequestedRegion` blocks every Regional API call outside the two allowed Regions for all principals in the OU, and account administrators cannot remove an SCP.
- ✗ **D. Permissions boundaries:** boundaries must be attached to each principal, and administrators in the account can create new roles without one or detach it. It is not a guardrail they are unable to bypass.

## Key idea
To restrict Regions for everyone in an account, including admins, use an SCP on aws:RequestedRegion with a NotAction exception for global services, not per-principal policies or detective rules.

stem: A SaaS monitoring vendor asks each customer to create an IAM role that the vendor's AWS account can assume to read CloudWatch metrics. The customer's security team is worried that another vendor customer could trick the vendor into using this role by supplying the customer's role ARN. What should the customer add to the role?

choices.text: A trust policy condition requiring aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent to be true for every AssumeRole call from the vendor
A trust policy condition limiting aws:SourceIp to the public IP address ranges the vendor publishes for its platform
A permissions boundary on the role that limits it to cloudwatch:GetMetricData and cloudwatch:ListMetrics actions only
A trust policy condition requiring sts:ExternalId to equal the unique value the vendor assigned to this customer

explanation:
## The confused deputy problem
A "deputy" is a service that acts for many clients, such as a vendor whose single AWS account assumes roles in hundreds of customer accounts. If customer X can type customer Y's role ARN into the vendor's console, the vendor would assume Y's role on X's behalf. The vendor was "confused" into misusing its own trusted identity.
## How the external ID fixes it
- The vendor generates a unique, non-secret identifier for each customer, for example `ext-4f1a92`.
- The customer's role trust policy trusts the vendor account and adds `"Condition": {"StringEquals": {"sts:ExternalId": "ext-4f1a92"}}`.
- The vendor always passes the external ID of the customer who is logged in to its console.
When X enters Y's ARN, the vendor sends X's external ID, the condition fails, and the assumption is denied.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. MFA condition:** the vendor's automated service calls `AssumeRole` without a human present, so requiring MFA would break the integration. It also does not tell the vendor which customer the request is for.
- ✗ **B. Source IP condition:** the confused deputy attack goes through the vendor's own platform, so the calls still come from the vendor's published IP ranges and the condition would allow them.
- ✗ **C. Permissions boundary:** limiting actions reduces what can be read, but the other customer could still read these metrics through the vendor. The problem is who triggers the assumption, not how much the role can do.
- ✓ **D. External ID in the trust policy (correct):** the vendor generates a unique ID per customer and always sends it on `AssumeRole`. Another customer who enters this customer's role ARN in the vendor console gets their own external ID sent, which does not match, so the vendor cannot be used as a confused deputy.

## Key idea
For third-party cross-account roles, the external ID stops the confused deputy problem; permissions and network conditions do not, because the vendor itself is the caller.

stem: An application on EC2 in Account A must assume a role in Account B. The role's trust policy lists arn:aws:iam::<Account-A-ID>:root as the principal. The instance profile role in Account A has only S3 permissions. The AssumeRole call returns AccessDenied. What is the MOST likely fix?

choices.text: Add sts:AssumeRole on the Account B role ARN to the identity policy of the instance profile role in Account A
Replace the trust policy principal with the ARN of the EC2 service so that instances in any account can assume the role
Add a resource-based policy to the role in Account B that allows sts:GetSessionToken for principals in Account A
Enable IAM Access Analyzer in Account B so that it can approve the cross-account trust relationship for the role

explanation:
## Cross-account access has two halves
When a principal in Account A calls `sts:AssumeRole` on a role in Account B, AWS checks:
- **Account B's side**: the role's trust policy must allow the caller. It can name a specific role ARN or the whole account, written as `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root`.
- **Account A's side**: the caller's own identity-based policies must allow `sts:AssumeRole` on `arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/ReadReports`.
## What "trusting the account root" means
`:root` does not mean only the root user. It means "any principal in that account that its administrators have allowed". The trust policy hands the final say to Account A's IAM policies. If those policies do not allow the call, the request fails with AccessDenied, even though the trust policy looks correct.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Identity policy in the caller's account (correct):** trusting `arn:aws:iam::<Account-A-ID>:root` delegates the decision to Account A's administrators. Account A must still grant `sts:AssumeRole` on the target role ARN to the instance role; without that allow, the call is denied even though the trust policy matches.
- ✗ **B. Trust the EC2 service principal:** `ec2.amazonaws.com` is used for roles that instances in the same account wear through an instance profile. It would not let a role in Account A assume the role, and trusting the service broadly would weaken security.
- ✗ **C. Allow GetSessionToken:** `GetSessionToken` returns temporary credentials for the caller's own identity and is not how cross-account access works. The role's trust policy is already its resource-based policy, and it already allows Account A.
- ✗ **D. Access Analyzer approval:** IAM Access Analyzer reports resources shared outside the account or organization. It has no approval step and does not change whether an `AssumeRole` call is allowed.

## Key idea
Cross-account role assumption needs both sides: the target role's trust policy must trust the caller, and the caller's identity policy must allow sts:AssumeRole on that role.

stem: A company has 200 project teams. Engineers sign in through IAM Identity Center, and each engineer's department and project are sent as attributes from the corporate IdP. The company wants engineers to manage only EC2 instances tagged with their own project, without writing a new policy for every new project. Which TWO actions meet this requirement? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Create a separate permission set per project that lists the instance ARNs belonging to that project's team
Attach an SCP per project OU that allows only EC2 actions on instances in the same OU as the engineer
Enable attributes for access control in IAM Identity Center so the project attribute is passed as a session tag
Create an AWS Resource Groups group for each project and grant engineers access to their project's group
Write one permission set policy that allows EC2 actions when aws:ResourceTag/project equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/project}

explanation:
## RBAC versus ABAC
- **Role-based access control (RBAC)** writes a policy per job or team, often listing specific resource ARNs. It grows with every new team.
- **Attribute-based access control (ABAC)** writes one policy that compares attributes (tags) of the caller with tags on the resource.
## How ABAC works with IAM Identity Center
1. The IdP (for example Okta or Microsoft Entra ID) sends user attributes such as `project=atlas`.
2. With **attributes for access control** enabled, Identity Center passes them as session tags, visible to policies as `aws:PrincipalTag/project`.
3. The permission set contains a condition like `"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceTag/project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/project}"}`.
An engineer tagged `atlas` can stop an instance tagged `project=atlas` but not one tagged `project=orion`. A new project only needs new tags, not new policies.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Permission set per project:** this is role-based access control. Every new project or new instance means editing or creating a permission set, which is exactly the growth problem the company wants to avoid.
- ✗ **B. SCP per project OU:** SCPs never grant permissions, so an SCP gives engineers no access by itself. It would also need a new OU and SCP for every project, which is the growth problem the company wants to avoid.
- ✓ **C. Attributes for access control (correct):** this passes the IdP's `project` attribute into each session as the principal tag `aws:PrincipalTag/project`, so the value is available to policies.
- ✗ **D. Resource Groups:** a resource group is a way to view and act on tagged resources. It is not an authorization mechanism, so membership in a group grants no permissions.
- ✓ **E. One tag-matching policy (correct):** a single statement that compares `aws:ResourceTag/project` with `${aws:PrincipalTag/project}` works for all 200 projects and for any new project, because the match is computed at request time.

## Key idea
ABAC scales by comparing a principal tag with a resource tag in one policy; RBAC needs a new role or permission set for every new project.

stem: EC2 instances in private subnets use an S3 gateway endpoint. Security is worried that a compromised instance could copy data to an S3 bucket in an attacker's personal AWS account through the endpoint. How can the company block this path while keeping access to its own buckets?

choices.text: Add a security group outbound rule that allows HTTPS only to the S3 managed prefix list and denies all other outbound traffic
Attach a VPC endpoint policy that allows S3 actions only when aws:ResourceOrgID matches the company's organization ID
Add a network ACL outbound rule that denies HTTPS to all S3 IP ranges except the ones assigned to the company's own buckets
Add a bucket policy on each company bucket that denies requests whose aws:SourceVpce value does not match the gateway endpoint ID

explanation:
## Two policies, two directions
Traffic from a private subnet to S3 through a gateway endpoint can be controlled at two points:
- **Bucket policy** (on the destination): "Which callers may use my bucket?" A condition on `aws:SourceVpce` lets the bucket accept requests only from a specific endpoint.
- **VPC endpoint policy** (on the path): "Which S3 resources may traffic from this VPC reach?" It applies to every request through the endpoint, whatever the bucket.
## Why network controls fail here
S3 is a shared service. All buckets in a Region answer on the same IP ranges, published as the managed prefix list `pl-xxxxxxxx`. Security groups and NACLs see only IPs and ports, never bucket names or owners.
## Example endpoint policy condition
`"Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceOrgID": "o-a1b2c3d4e5"}}` allows S3 calls only to buckets owned by accounts in the organization. A `PutObject` to `s3://attacker-bucket` is denied at the endpoint. In practice, add explicit exceptions for any AWS-owned buckets the instances need, such as OS package repositories.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Security group with prefix list:** the S3 prefix list contains the IP ranges for all of S3 in the Region. Every bucket, including the attacker's, is served from those same addresses, so the rule cannot tell buckets apart.
- ✓ **B. VPC endpoint policy on the resource's organization (correct):** the endpoint policy is evaluated for every request going through the endpoint. Allowing S3 actions only when `aws:ResourceOrgID` equals the company's organization means requests to a bucket owned by any other account are denied, while company buckets keep working.
- ✗ **C. NACL with S3 IP ranges:** S3 does not assign dedicated IP addresses per bucket or per customer, so there are no "company bucket" ranges to allow. The same endpoints serve every account.
- ✗ **D.:** Bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce: this controls who can reach the company's buckets, not which buckets the instances can reach. The attacker's bucket has its own policy, so this does nothing to stop uploads to it.

## Key idea
Bucket policies decide who may reach your bucket; the VPC endpoint policy decides which buckets your VPC may reach, which is what stops exfiltration.

stem: A company serves a web application through Amazon CloudFront with an Application Load Balancer as the origin. Security requires that the ALB is not reachable from the internet at all, and only this CloudFront distribution may send it traffic. Which solution meets the requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.text: Keep the ALB internet-facing and add network ACL rules that allow only the CloudFront IP ranges, updated by a scheduled function
Keep the ALB internet-facing and attach an AWS WAF web ACL that blocks requests from every country except the CloudFront edge countries
Keep the ALB internet-facing and allow inbound HTTPS only from the CloudFront origin-facing managed prefix list in its security group
Move the ALB to private subnets as an internal load balancer and register it as a CloudFront VPC origin for the distribution

explanation:
## Ways to lock an ALB behind CloudFront
- **Public ALB + prefix list**: the security group allows `com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing`. This limits traffic to CloudFront servers, but every customer's distribution uses the same servers, so a custom secret header checked by the ALB is usually added too.
- **VPC origin**: CloudFront connects to an internal ALB, NLB or EC2 instance in a private subnet. The load balancer is never exposed to the internet, and there is no header secret to rotate.
## Example layout
- `internal-app-alb` in two private subnets, security group allowing HTTPS from the CloudFront VPC origin.
- The distribution uses the VPC origin as its origin; users reach `www.example.com` only through CloudFront, where WAF and caching apply.
With no public endpoint, scanners and attackers have nothing to hit directly, which is the strongest form of "only through CloudFront".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. NACL with CloudFront ranges:** NACLs have a small rule limit, CloudFront publishes many ranges that change, and the scheduled updater is extra code to run. The ALB would still be internet-facing and reachable from any distribution.
- ✗ **B. WAF geo blocking:** CloudFront edge locations are in most countries, so geography does not identify CloudFront traffic. Attackers in allowed countries could still reach the public ALB directly.
- ✗ **C. Managed prefix list in security group:** the ALB is still internet-facing, and the prefix list covers all CloudFront edge servers, including distributions owned by other AWS customers. Anyone could point their own distribution at the ALB.
- ✓ **D. CloudFront VPC origin (correct):** CloudFront can deliver to an internal ALB in private subnets through a VPC origin. The ALB has no public IP address, so it cannot be reached from the internet, and only CloudFront, through the VPC origin, can connect to it.

## Key idea
To make an origin truly private behind CloudFront, use a VPC origin with an internal ALB; a prefix list only narrows a public ALB to all of CloudFront.

stem: A company wants to remove bastion hosts and stop opening port 22. Administrators must get shell access to Amazon Linux 2023 instances in private subnets that have no NAT gateway or internet access, and all sessions must be logged. Which TWO steps are required? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Allow inbound TCP port 22 in the instance security groups from the Systems Manager service IP address ranges
Create interface VPC endpoints for Systems Manager (ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages) in the private subnets' VPC
Associate an Elastic IP address with each instance so the Session Manager service can initiate the connection
Store each instance's SSH private key in AWS Secrets Manager so Session Manager can retrieve it during login
Attach an instance profile whose role includes the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy to each instance

explanation:
## How Session Manager works
AWS Systems Manager Session Manager gives an interactive shell without SSH. The SSM Agent on the instance opens an **outbound** HTTPS (443) connection to Systems Manager and keeps it open. When an administrator starts a session from the console or `aws ssm start-session`, traffic flows over that existing channel.
## What an instance needs
- **The agent**: preinstalled on Amazon Linux 2023 and many other AMIs.
- **Permissions**: an instance profile role with `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` (or the account-wide Default Host Management Configuration).
- **Network path**: a NAT gateway, or, for isolated subnets, interface endpoints `com.amazonaws.<region>.ssm` and `.ssmmessages`, plus `.ec2messages` for older agent versions. Sending session output to CloudWatch Logs or S3 also needs a `logs` interface endpoint or an S3 gateway endpoint.
## Why it is more secure
- No inbound rules, no bastion host, no SSH keys.
- Who may start a session is decided by IAM, and every session is recorded in CloudTrail; session output can be sent to CloudWatch Logs or S3.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Open port 22:** Session Manager needs no inbound ports at all. The agent makes an outbound HTTPS connection, so opening SSH would only add attack surface.
- ✓ **B. Systems Manager interface endpoints (correct):** with no NAT or internet, the agent needs private endpoints to reach the service: `ssm` and `ssmmessages`, plus `ec2messages`, which older agent versions still use. Session activity is recorded in CloudTrail, and session output can be sent to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
- ✗ **C. Elastic IP per instance:** Session Manager never connects inbound to the instance, and a public IP does nothing in a subnet without an internet gateway route. It would expose the instances for no benefit.
- ✗ **D. SSH keys in Secrets Manager:** Session Manager does not use SSH keys. Access is controlled by IAM policies on the user, which removes key distribution and rotation entirely.
- ✓ **E. Instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore (correct):** the SSM Agent (preinstalled on Amazon Linux 2023) uses this role to register the instance and open the session channel.

## Key idea
Session Manager replaces bastions with an outbound agent connection: give the instance an SSM role and a path to the SSM endpoints; no inbound ports, public IPs or SSH keys.

stem: A Lambda function was attached to private subnets so it can query an RDS database. Since then, its calls to AWS Secrets Manager to read the database password time out after 3 seconds. The VPC has no NAT gateway, and the secret's permissions have not changed. What should the solutions architect do?

choices.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager with private DNS and allow HTTPS from the function's security group
Increase the function timeout to 60 seconds and add retries with backoff to the SDK client that calls Secrets Manager
Enable the option to assign a public IP address to the function's network interfaces and add a route to an internet gateway
Add a resource policy to the secret that grants the function's execution role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret

explanation:
## What changes when Lambda joins a VPC
By default a function runs in a Lambda-managed network with internet access. When you attach it to your subnets, Lambda creates elastic network interfaces there, and all outbound traffic follows those subnets' route tables and security groups.
## Reaching AWS APIs from private subnets
Services such as Secrets Manager, SQS or STS are public endpoints like `secretsmanager.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`. From a private subnet you reach them through:
- a **NAT gateway** (per-hour and per-GB charges, traffic leaves through the internet gateway), or
- an **interface VPC endpoint** (AWS PrivateLink), which puts private IPs for the service in your subnets.
## Private DNS
With private DNS enabled on the endpoint, the standard service name resolves to the endpoint's private IPs, so no code change is needed. The endpoint's security group must allow TCP 443 from the function's security group.
## Reading the symptom
AccessDenied means the request arrived and was refused. A timeout means it never arrived.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Secrets Manager interface endpoint (correct):** once a function runs in a VPC, its traffic follows the subnets' routes, and these have no path to the public Secrets Manager endpoint. An interface endpoint with private DNS makes the normal endpoint name resolve to private IPs inside the VPC, so the SDK works unchanged.
- ✗ **B. Longer timeout and retries:** there is no network path, so every attempt will hang until it times out. Waiting longer only increases cost and latency.
- ✗ **C. Public IP for the function:** Lambda network interfaces in a VPC never receive public IPs, even in a public subnet, so an internet gateway route does not give the function internet access.
- ✗ **D. Secret resource policy:** a permission problem would return AccessDenied immediately, not a timeout. The stem also states the permissions have not changed; the request is not reaching the service.

## Key idea
A timeout from a VPC-attached Lambda means no network path; add a VPC endpoint (or NAT), since Lambda in a VPC never gets a public IP.

stem: An internal HR API built on Amazon API Gateway must be callable only by applications running in one specific VPC. It must not be reachable from the internet, even with valid credentials. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: An edge-optimized REST API that requires IAM authorization and a policy allowing only roles used by applications in the VPC
A Regional REST API with an AWS WAF web ACL that allows only the VPC's NAT gateway Elastic IP address as the source of requests
An HTTP API with a Lambda authorizer that inspects the X-Forwarded-For header and rejects addresses outside the VPC CIDR
A private REST API reached through an execute-api interface endpoint, with a resource policy allowing only that endpoint's ID

explanation:
## API Gateway endpoint types
- **Edge-optimized**: public, fronted by CloudFront edge locations.
- **Regional**: public, served from one Region.
- **Private**: no public endpoint; reachable only through an interface VPC endpoint for `execute-api`. Only REST APIs support this type.
## Locking a private API to one VPC
1. Create an interface endpoint `com.amazonaws.<region>.execute-api` in the VPC.
2. Attach a resource policy to the API, for example allow `execute-api:Invoke` only when `aws:SourceVpce` equals `vpce-0abc123`.
3. Deploy the API so the resource policy takes effect.
A request from another VPC, even one with its own execute-api endpoint, fails the condition and is denied. Authentication (IAM, Cognito, Lambda authorizers) can still be added on top to decide which applications in the VPC may call it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Edge-optimized API with IAM auth:** IAM authorization checks who calls, not where from. Anyone holding valid credentials for those roles could call the public endpoint from anywhere, which the stem forbids.
- ✗ **B. Regional API with WAF IP allowlist:** the API is still public on the internet, and the allowlist depends on traffic leaving through the NAT gateway. The endpoint remains discoverable and the design fails if routing changes.
- ✗ **C. HTTP API with header check:** the API is public, and `X-Forwarded-For` can be spoofed by the client. HTTP APIs also do not support the private endpoint type.
- ✓ **D. Private REST API with execute-api endpoint (correct):** a private API has no public endpoint at all. Clients in the VPC reach it through an interface endpoint for `execute-api`, and the resource policy's `aws:SourceVpce` condition limits calls to that one endpoint, so other VPCs and the internet cannot invoke it.

## Key idea
For an API reachable only from a VPC, use a private REST API with an execute-api interface endpoint and a resource policy on aws:SourceVpce; authentication alone does not remove the public endpoint.

stem: An application encrypts sensitive fields with AWS KMS before writing them to a DynamoDB global table replicated between us-east-1 and eu-west-1. During a regional outage of us-east-1, the application in eu-west-1 must still decrypt every item without calling us-east-1. Which approach meets this requirement?

choices.text: Rely on the AWS owned key that DynamoDB uses for encryption at rest, because global table replicas decrypt items automatically
Create a single-Region customer managed key in us-east-1 and grant the eu-west-1 application role permission to call kms:Decrypt on it
Create a KMS multi-Region primary key in us-east-1 with a replica key in eu-west-1 and decrypt with the local key in each Region
Create single-Region customer managed keys in both Regions and import the same key material into each key so they are interchangeable

explanation:
## Why client-side encryption needs care across Regions
DynamoDB already encrypts tables at rest. Some applications additionally encrypt fields such as `ssn` themselves (client-side) before writing. That ciphertext is replicated byte for byte to every global table replica, so each Region must be able to decrypt it.
## Single-Region versus multi-Region keys
- A **single-Region key** lives in one Region. Ciphertext it creates can be decrypted only by calling KMS in that Region.
